84.title: Feature-branch staging
84.content: Skill feature-staging: Manages feature-branch staging deployments under gh-pages/branches// for before/after publication review comparison. Handles branch creation, staging deployment, commit SHA stamping, and cleanup. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release, Adjudicate two KG extractors, GuidelineKG nightly path: verify and adjudicate the result, GuidelineKG nightly path: prepare the work order, GuidelineKG nightly path .

85.title: When to use this skill
85.content: When a content change is being reviewed and the reviewer (or the author) needs to see the rendered result before merging. The staging deployment puts the feature branch’s rendered site at: . https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/branches/<branch-slug>/ . A preview is the general publication step with a different root. The push itself is render-kg-to-cdn with branches/<branch-slug>/ as the publication root URL and the gh-pages Tool as the target — the same step a release takes with the site root. What this skill owns is everything around that call: the slug, the banner and staging.json, the render log, the PR comment, and taking the preview down. Which site — the repository the change lives in . <owner>/<repo> above is the repository that holds the change, not the repository of the index the agent happens to be working in. Read that repository’s index.config.json first: . | the change lives in | its preview is at | published by | . | a repository with its own site (its index.config.json has a site entry) | https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/branches/<slug>/, and the root from its default branch | that repository: stage-local.ts --repo . from its checkout when it declares site.agentRun (below), else its own staging.yml | . | a layer an index mounts and publishes as part of its own site (no site of its own) | branches/<slug>/ on the index’s site | a staging re-pin: a pull request on the index that points the mount at the branch’s commit, recorded with bun run cat mount:remote --staging (basis staging, no consent needed) | . A repository with a site of its own is previewed there, even when an index also mounts it. The index’s site shows it as one layer among its layers, which is the wrong page for that repository’s reviewers. If the repository’s own build cannot run yet (its publisher refuses for a missing cache or an undeclared input), say what is missing and ask. Never fall back to the index’s site in silence.

86.title: How it works
86.content: 1. Feature branch → staging deployment . When an agent pushes to a feature branch with an open pull request, drafts included, feature-staging.yml automatically: . | Builds the docs site (Jekyll + TypeDoc + BPMN diagrams) | Writes the build’s facts — commit SHA, timestamp, branch, PR, issue, build log — once, to staging.json at the preview root | Injects a constant staging banner at the top of every HTML page, which reads those facts in the browser | Comments on the PR that the preview is staged and queued, with the earliest push time and when it should be live | Waits for the rate-limit window (§8), then deploys to gh-pages/branches/<branch-slug>/ only the files that differ from the live site (staging-share.ts apply). The preview’s staging-sw.js serves the rest from the live site in the browser and puts the banner back on its pages; the live site’s root 404.html (staging-share.ts write-404, written by docs-site.yml) installs that worker for a deep link opened before it exists. A page is shared only when it matches the live one once the per-preview edits are set aside (banner, SEO strip, fa-staging and fa-search-index, TypeDoc’s title suffix); anything else keeps the preview’s own copy. The footer build stamp is filled in the browser on every build, the live site’s from build.json, so an unchanged page is byte-identical across deploys | Rewrites the same comment: pushed at a time, live by about five minutes later | . 2. The staging banner . Every staged page carries a muted-sage banner: . 🔀 FEATURE BRANCH — claude/update-schedule · commit a1b2c3d · built 2026-09-18T00:30:00Z · PR #42 · issue #215 · compare with main ↗ · build log . Its colour, #4F6F52, measures 5.63:1 against its white text, above the 4.5:1 WCAG AA threshold. Check any replacement the same way; the pale decorator sages (#9CAF88, #87A96B) land near 2.5:1. The facts are fetched, not baked — and that is a storage decision . cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-banner.ts injects a fragment that is byte-identical on every page and across every rebuild, and the browser derives its preview root from location.pathname, fetches staging.json and fills the banner in. A per-build value in the fragment makes every page unique on every build, so each re-push adds the whole site to gh-pages as new objects. Three rules: . | Nothing per-build may go back into the fragment. staging-banner-constant.test.ts runs two builds with different facts and compares the emitted bytes, so any leak fails regardless of how it is spelled. Add the fact to staging.json instead. | A failed fetch must still say PREVIEW. The static markup carries “FEATURE BRANCH” before any fetch happens, and the fetch only ever ADDS detail. “Could not determine” is never rendered as “this is the real site” — the same third-state rule the rest of the repository runs on, and here the failure mode is a reviewer approving the wrong artefact. | Every value from the JSON goes in as textContent, never as markup. Git ref names may contain <, > and " — they are not in git’s forbidden set, which stops at space, ~, ^, :, ?, *, [, \ and the control characters. staging-banner.e2e.ts pins this with a branch name carrying an onerror payload. | . Pages still differ between previews, because Jekyll’s relative_url prepends the baseurl to ~235 hrefs per page and the fa-translation-index island publishes site.baseurl to JavaScript. Both are coupled to the language switcher. 3. Commit SHA stamping — and the four fields staging must NOT write . Both builds write docs/_data/build.yml, and they do not write the same fields. The difference is deliberate: it is the second half of the deduplication above. |   | docs-site.yml (main) | feature-staging.yml (a preview) | . | sha, short_sha, built_at, run_url | written | DELIBERATELY ABSENT | . | branch, staging, staging_slug, pr_number, search_index | — | written | . Why staging omits them. site-chrome/_includes/footer_custom.html renders short_sha, built_at and run_url into the footer of every page, so writing them per build changes every page on every deploy. The client fills those three in from the same staging.json the banner already fetches — one request, two consumers — and a failed fetch leaves Jekyll’s | default: 'dev' in place rather than blanking the footer, which is the same third state §”The facts are fetched, not baked” requires of the banner. On main there is one copy and nothing to deduplicate, so the include’s own reason stands: “a stale browser cache and a deploy that has not run look identical.” . Adding a per-build field back to the staging stamp will not fail a test. staging-banner-constant.test.ts compares the banner fragment, which is genuinely constant; the footer is not in it, because it lives in a Jekyll include rather than in the workflow’s injection step. Check the deploy commits on gh-pages, not the code, to confirm pages do not differ across rebuilds. A Jekyll layout can read site.data.build.sha to display the deployed version — on main. Under a preview, read it from staging.json. 4. Before/after comparison . The reviewer opens both URLs side by side: . | Surface | URL | What it shows | . | Main (current) | <pages-url>/ | The published state on main | . | Staging (proposed) | <pages-url>/branches/<slug>/ | The feature branch’s changes | . The commit SHA on each page confirms exactly what is being compared. 5. Cleanup . When the PR is merged or closed, the cleanup job in feature-staging.yml removes branches/<slug>/ from gh-pages so stale previews don’t accumulate. The full retention rules — merged vs closed-unmerged, the label, the dispatch — are in staging-review §”Staging retention”. 6. The cap — 3 GB of previews in total, the oldest rotated off . Previews are capped by size, at 3 GB in total, and the oldest are rotated off. The cap is by size rather than count because one preview can run to hundreds of megabytes. Per-PR cleanup bounds nothing in total, every preview is a full copy of the site, and a gh-pages branch past GitHub’s 10 GB Pages limit freezes the live site. So every stage run, inside its push loop, runs cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-rotate.ts: it stamps the preview it is staging (branches/<slug>/.staged-at), keeps that one plus the most recently updated others while the total fits MAX_PREVIEW_BYTES (3 GB, 3 x 1024^3 bytes, defined there and nowhere else), and removes the rest, oldest first — each with a removed render-log entry, its record retired into branches/_retired/, and a line (slug, age, size) in the commit message and job log. _retired/ and non-preview entries are never touched. Two things to know when editing it: . | The push loop re-reads gh-pages on every attempt; it does not rebase. The commit carries removals decided against one read of the branch, and a replayed removal is a stale one — it could delete a preview another run has just refreshed. Same shape as publish-gh-pages.sh. | A rotated-off preview is regenerated by the next push to its PR branch. It can reach an OPEN PR’s preview; the cost is a 404 until the author pushes, not lost work. Detail and the reviewer’s remedy: staging-review §”The cap”. | . 7. The cone — a preview rebuilds only what a changed file can reach . A preview rebuilds only the dependency cone of the changed files, at FILE level, with each derived directory’s generator declared as writer. The rule is general across rendered kinds. A rendered directory is in the cone when a changed file is . | under its own path (its pages, or its source data), or | in the import closure of a writer it declares, or under a writer directory (a path ending in /: what a generator reads, such as its templates, rather than imports), or | in a directory it is derivedFrom, transitively (check:derived-from --downstream <instance/id> prints that half on its own). | . cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-cone.ts computes it; compose-docs.ts carriedInstances applies it to the composed layers. Three rules: . | Any doubt carries. No file list, a writer that does not exist, or an import that does not resolve carries the directory, with the reason in the build log. A preview missing the pages under review misleads a reviewer, while an oversized one only costs bytes. | A computed import() is bounded, not ignored. It can load only a module, so it carries on a changed module file and never on a page. The two such sites a generator reaches today (harness-config.ts’s contributes loader and block-module.ts’s block loader) have DECLARED targets and are walked exactly; DECLARED_COMPUTED_IMPORTS lists them. | The instance-prefix match is a floor. The cone can only add to it. Narrowing below it is a separate decision, made once the cone has been measured in previews. | . A skill-only change carries no IG; a change to gen-ig-pages.ts or to the DAK layer’s themes/chrome.json carries all three. staging-cone.test.ts holds these cases as tests. Built sites follow the same rule. An IG’s own Jekyll site and its AST site are BUILT in the preview from an upstream repository pinned in the layer’s own files, not composed from the checkout. stage-ig-sites.ts and stage-ast-sites.ts take --changed-files and stage only the layers siteInCone reaches. Its reasons, in order: no file list; a change to the build environment (SITE_ENVIRONMENT: the docs Gemfile and this workflow); a change under the layer; the cone reaching any of the layer’s directories (a theme change arrives this way); or a change in the stager’s closure. Each decision is printed with its reason. When you add a generated directory, declare its writer and derivedFrom. Without them the cone cannot reach it through code or data, and the prefix floor is all it gets. 8. The rate limit — a preview never cancels the main site’s Pages build . Staging previews are pushed to gh-pages at a limited rate. GitHub’s pages build and deployment keeps only the NEWEST run, so every push cancels the build in flight, the main site’s included; a build takes about three minutes. So before each push attempt the stage job re-reads gh-pages and runs cat-harness-tools/scripts/staging-push-gate.ts gate, which holds the push until the branch tip is old enough: . | tip of gh-pages | wait until it is | . | a staging commit (staging(...)) | STAGING_WINDOW_MS — 5 min | . | anything else: the main-site publish, publish.yml, any other publisher | MAIN_WINDOW_MS — 10 min | . The numbers live once, in that script. Exit 75 means it slept until the window should open (plus up to a minute of jitter) and the loop must re-read and ask again; exit 1 means the job has waited MAX_WAIT_MS (two hours) and fails rather than pushing; exit 2 is an unreadable tip, never read as open. Three things to know when editing it: . | git’s fast-forward rule is the lock. Two jobs that both find the window open both build on the same tip; one push is rejected, re-reads, finds a tip younger than the window, and waits. So at most one staging push lands per window with no shared state. A rejection whose tip MOVED is therefore a lost race, sent back to the gate without spending one of the three attempts; only a rejection with the tip unmoved counts as a failure. | No concurrency group, and none should be added. Every waiting preview would pend in one group and each arrival would cancel the last. The per-branch group at the workflow level stays: a newer push to the same PR cancels a preview still waiting at the gate, so a superseded preview is never pushed at all. | A staging push BEFORE a main-site push is harmless; only one AFTER it cancels the build that matters. The main push then cancels the staging build, and the build that runs carries both. That is why the gate looks at the tip, and why it does not wait for docs-site runs that have not pushed yet. | . A rate limit is used rather than a batching flush job because the gate is one script and one loop whose correctness rests on git, while a flush job needs a second workflow, an artifact round trip per preview, a record of what is deployed, a best-effort schedule and a write token over content built from a pull request. The cost is latency under load: with K previews waiting, the last one pushes about 5 × K minutes later, and the PR comment gives its own estimate. The cleanup and cleanup-dispatch jobs do NOT pass through the gate. They push once per closed PR rather than once per push. 9. Build types — preview and full . There are two build types. A public comment (PC) build is a full build, and so is a release. | build type | used for | builds | . | preview | every pull request’s branches/<slug>/ preview | only what the change can reach (the cone, §7); every whole-corpus index is main’s copy, put back rather than rebuilt | . | full | the main site deploy, a public comment release, a release | everything; every index rebuilt from the tree being published | . An index is computed over the whole corpus: the search index, the LSI viewer, the SQLite slices, the handler index, the glossary pages, the translation status pages and the node-kind pages. A builtAtPublish entry says so with index: true; a writer is borrowed only when every entry it writes says so. Rebuilding an index in a preview shows the reviewer almost nothing and costs minutes, so in a preview derive:publish puts back main’s copy from main’s writer-cone recording and logs borrowed <writer>; the search index is served from main the same way (§”Serve the published search index” in the preview workflow). So a preview of a glossary, translation or node-kind change shows main’s copy of those pages: review such a change on a full build (dispatch with build_type: full) or in its source. The switch is CAT_BUILD_TYPE (cat-harness-tools/scripts/lib/build-type.ts). Any doubt builds full: unset means full, and a value that is neither word is refused. A preview whose main recording holds no copy of an index builds it. A public comment release must be frozen from a full build. A frozen release is cited by page and line for the whole comment period, so its search and slices must describe the draft, not main. Dispatch the preview workflow for the branch with build_type: full, then run pc:release freeze. Freeze refuses a copy whose staging.json says buildType: "preview", and records the build type in release.json. 10. Agent-built previews — deferred on the critical path, verified by a full CI rebuild . When an agent builds and pushes a preview with stage-local.ts, it writes branches/<slug>/_build-record.json (scripts/preview-record.ts) recording builder: "agent", the git tree hash tree of the source tree it built (HEAD^{tree} or the merge tree with origin/main), the head and base commit SHAs, and the SHA-256 of every deployed file outside the per-build metadata (staging.json, _build-record.json, .staged-at, build.yml). When feature-staging.yml runs on the pull request: . | Defer on the critical path. conflict-gate checks branches/<slug>/_build-record.json on gh-pages. When builder is "agent" and record.tree equals MERGE_SHA^{tree} (refs/pull/<n>/merge), the preview is already live for that exact merge tree: the workflow sets the preview/agent-build commit status on the PR head to pending, posts a <!-- preview-build-verify --> notice on the PR, and skips the critical-path stage build so the runner is free. Any missing record, CI-built record, or tree mismatch (including when main moved under the branch) builds on the critical path as usual. | Verify off the critical path. preview-verify-sweep.yml (triggered when feature-staging.yml completes and on a 15-minute schedule) checks that no Feature Staging run is queued or in progress, finds the oldest open PR whose head commit has preview/agent-build in state pending, and dispatches feature-staging.yml with verify_pr=<number>. | Compare or replace. The verify run rebuilds refs/pull/<n>/merge in full and runs preview-record.ts compare against the agent’s _build-record.json on gh-pages: . | Files match (same=true): nothing is redeployed; preview/agent-build is set to success (or failure if a built-site check failed) and the PR comment records the verified tree. | Files differ (same=false) or the base moved (same=stale): CI’s build is deployed to branches/<slug>/ (guarded so a newer preview tree is never overwritten) with a rendered log entry, and when the agent’s build differed, preview/agent-build is set to failure with the differing file paths listed in the PR comment. | Merge guard: merge-guard check 5 (src/coordinator/merge-guard.ts) reads preview/agent-build alongside check runs; pending holds the PR as not ready, and failure refuses the merge. | . | .

87.title: Agent workflow
87.content: When an author requests a content change: . | Detect scope — use content-graph and integration-watcher to identify affected blocks and downstream implications | Create feature branch — branch from main, open PR immediately | Make changes — edit content blocks, deterministic logic, translations | Push — on a folio whose staging.yml runs on push, the staging deployment happens automatically. On an agent-run repository, run stage-local.ts (below). | Report staging URL — tell the author the preview is at <pages-url>/branches/<slug>/ | Iterate — each push updates the staging deployment with a new SHA | . The BPMN for this workflow is the content core’s processes/content/content-change-review.bpmn. Publishing without a runner — stage-local.ts, one command . When the Actions queue is backed up, the agent can build and publish itself: it already has the checkout, the platform and bun. On an agent-run repository (below) this is not a shortcut. It is the only publish path. It is one command for a preview and for the main site, for a folio and for a FHIR IG: . bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --plan # what it would do; nothing built bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --dry-run # build, compose the commit, push nothing bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> # build and push bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/stage-local.ts --repo <repo> --artifact <dir> . It prints its plan first, every time: which workflow it mirrors, where the output lands, what it replaces and what it keeps, the commit message, and what it does not run. The size review. Owner, 2026-11-10: “add size review as part of authoring process”. Every build, preview or main, prints a size report before its push (site-size.ts, bun run cat site:size). The report gives the total against the published root, the top directories, the size by extension, the biggest files, byte-identical duplicates, source maps, the directories named after another layer of index.lock.json, and the directories the shared-assets host could serve. It writes site-size.json beside the build, never into the site. The review is advisory: growth over 10% or 10 MB is a warning, and nothing is refused. Read the report before you hand over the preview. The usual culprits each have one fix: . | another layer’s pages copied in: link that layer’s own site; | the same bytes under several names: publish one index, and serve each file once; | vendored libraries: serve them from the shared-assets host; | .map files: do not publish them. | . When the growth holds and none of these fixes applies, raise a decision card with the owner, with the comparison line and the top contributing directories on it. Which publisher is read from the repository’s own workflow files, from the reusable workflow each one calls: . | a caller of folio-staging.yml is a folio. The build inputs (build_command, site_dir, publish_branch, …) are read from that caller. | a caller of a reusable workflow that a mounted layer declares as a site publisher is that publisher’s kind. The IG layer declares one: a caller of its fhirbuild.yml or ghbuild.yml is an IG, published by that layer’s own code, which stage-local.ts reaches through the layer’s declared site-publisher-ig pipeline slot and never by path. The reusable workflow is fetched at the ref the caller names, and its build job is run step by step as written: run: blocks with the environment a runner gives them, docker:// steps in their image. Steps that read a secret, push to the source branch, or need an Actions runtime are skipped, and the plan names each one with its reason. fhirbuild.yml itself only triggers build.fhir.org’s auto-build, so the Pages build is the ghbuild.yml beside it, and the plan says so. | a repository that calls both (smart-ra carries an IG under input/) gets the folio, unless --publisher ig is given. The folio owns the publish root. An IG’s root deploy is a clean one, and it is refused on a publish branch that holds a folio’s branches/, _render-log/ or _main-site.json. | . Main site or preview follows the branch, as the workflows do. The default branch publishes the main site; any other branch publishes a preview. --main says the same explicitly, and it is refused off the default branch. The main site is published only from a HEAD that is the pushed tip of the default branch. |   | folio | IG | . | preview | branches/<slug>/, replaced wholesale; held by the rate-limit gate (§8); commit staging(<slug>): from <sha>; render log staging-preview | branches/<last path component>/, nothing deleted; commit Deploy candidate branch | . | main site | the root, through publish-main-site.ts: only the files the last publish’s _main-site.json lists are replaced, and branches/, _render-log/ and anything a person put at the root are kept; commit main-site: from <sha>; render log main-site for / | the root, cleaned except for the deploy step’s clean-exclude (branches, sitepreview) and the action’s own exclusions; commit Deploy main branch | . Every path refuses an empty build before it deletes anything. | Pushing removes the first wait and not the second. Pages deploys on a runner, so say the page is live once that deploy has run, never sooner. | --artifact <dir>: no GitHub at all. It writes the same build as a bundle for a claude.ai Artifact: index.html plus the files listed in <dir>/artifact.json. Publish that, and it is live in about a minute, private until shared. | An Artifact holds at most 254 files plus the page per publish. Whole top-level directories are left out to fit, the ones with the most files first. artifact.json names each one, and links into a left-out directory 404. | Before publishing a folio whose content belongs to a real organisation (a WHO draft, say), ask the author: an Artifact is a new place that content appears. | . | What it does not do, and says in its plan: . | the folio preview’s QA sweep, screenshots, review-comment ingestion and PR comment (the banner says the preview was built locally); | the IG workflow’s PR comments, its branch-history page and README write-back (each reads a token, or writes the source branch); | the IG deploy action’s single-commit, which force-pushes one orphan commit and erases the publish branch’s history. This path commits on top and never force-pushes. | . | An IG build needs what its workflow needs. The workflow runs IG Publisher in a Docker image, so a machine with no Docker daemon gets the plan from --dry-run, and a real run stops naming the missing prerequisite. | An IG repository’s own site is built from its AST, not from the Publisher’s HTML. The repository declares site.build in its index.config.json entry (inline — never a <instance>.config.json), and that recipe’s first step restores the AST from its cache branch and refuses one that is not valid for the commit. The cache is refreshed by a Publisher run on a runner, through the IG layer’s reusable refresh workflow. It is the one workflow an agent-run IG repository dispatches, and only a person, or an agent the owner names for that run, dispatches it. The layer that owns IG builds owns the rule and the workflow; this skill names no IG step. | . Agent-run repositories — the GitHub Actions path is documented, not run . A repository is agent-run when it says so in its own index.config.json: "site": { "agentRun": true }. An agent builds and publishes its site, and its publish workflow keeps only workflow_dispatch. This skill keeps no list of them: the declaration is the list, and stage-local.ts says in every plan whether the repository declares it. For these repositories the GitHub Actions path is documentation. It says what the workflow does, so that the agent path can match it. It is not a fallback for an agent to take. | what | agent path | GitHub Actions path (documented, not run) | . | a folio preview at branches/<slug>/ | stage-local.ts from the branch | folio-staging.yml job stage | . | a folio’s main site at the Pages root | stage-local.ts from the default branch | folio-staging.yml job publish-main | . | an IG preview at branches/<branch>/ | stage-local.ts from the branch | the IG publisher’s ghbuild.yml, “Deploy candidate” | . | an IG’s main site at the Pages root | stage-local.ts from the default branch | the IG publisher’s ghbuild.yml, “Deploy main” | . | QA sweep, screenshots, review comments, PR comments | not run (the plan says so) | jobs in the workflows above | . Never dispatch the workflow, to cover a gap or for any other reason: a dispatched run contradicts the repository’s agent-run setting. When the agent path cannot do a step, say which step it is and ask. Skills that drive GitHub Actions are not to be implemented. Document what the workflows do, here and in the workflow files, so that an agent-run step can be checked against them — stage-local.ts reads the workflow files rather than restating them, so a change to a workflow’s build or layout is a change to the agent path too.

88.title: Staleness detection
88.content: The SHA stamp means staleness is always detectable: . | Staging matches PR head → the staging preview is current | Staging SHA ≠ PR head → the staging preview is stale (push again) | Main site SHA = merge commit → the publication is current | Main site SHA ≠ latest main → docs-site.yml needs to run | .

89.title: Example — a change that spans several blocks
89.content: An author needs to change the immunization schedule: . | Agent detects the change affects: . | Narrative content in the immunization chapter | Decision logic (CQL) for scheduling the next visit | Indicators that count doses administered | Referral logic for follow-up visits | . | Agent creates feature/update-immunization-schedule | Agent edits all affected blocks, assesses downstream impact | Push → staging deployment → author reviews | Author submits to the guidance review committee | Committee compares main vs branches/feature-update-immunization-schedule/ | Committee approves → merge → staging cleaned up → main site updated | .

90.title: Before you hand a staging URL to a person
90.content: Check the ref, then say how long and come back. A preview push is not a served page, and the bot’s “Staging preview” comment reports at most the first, not the second — and while it says queued, not even that. List branches/<slug>/ on refs/heads/gh-pages before relaying the URL; quote the comment’s own push and live-by times (the rate limit in §8 can hold a push for several windows), or say the stage job takes about 22 minutes plus the wait and Pages adds 3 to 4 on top; schedule the re-check rather than promising it. The three states, and why the third is not yours to assert, are in staging-review §”Before you hand a staging URL to a person (STRICT)”. It is the same rule and it is written once, there.

91.title: Before you report a staging URL as broken
91.content: Look at the publish ref, not the site. A staging URL is LOOKED UP in gh-pages under branches/<branch-slug>/, never composed from the source path — cat-harness/docs/guides/x.md publishes to /docs/cat-harness/guides/x.html, and composing it from the source path yields a 404 for a page that is there. From an agent container a curl against a Pages URL fails on the proxy regardless, so a failed fetch is not evidence either way. Full rule: github-state-inspection (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc).

92.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: feedback-deep-links.

94.title: Harness projections: CI writes them, the owner consents to every hand edit
94.content: Skill harness-projections: Who may write under .claude/, and when. The generated projections of the knowledge graph (.claude/commands/*.md from skill:commands, the assembled agent memory under .claude/agents/ and .claude/agent-memory/) are written by CI, which commits them to the PR branch, and never by an agent. A hand-edited .claude/ file (settings.json, its hooks, a hand-written command or agent definition) changes only with the owner’s explicit consent to that change: the agent shows the exact diff and the reason, asks first, and records the consent. Read before staging any path under .claude/. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release, Adjudicate two KG extractors, GuidelineKG nightly path: verify and adjudicate the result, GuidelineKG nightly path: prepare the work order, GuidelineKG nightly path .claude/ is what the Claude Code harness reads before any skill is loaded: the slash commands a person can type, the memory injected into a subagent, and the hooks and permissions every session runs under. An edit there changes how every later session behaves, including sessions that never see the commit.claude/ is one instance of a general rule. Every coding-agent Tool has config files, and some of them are projections of the graph: CI writes the projections, and a person consents to each hand edit.claude/ is named here because it is the agent-host directory the generators write. Which files a Tool reads, and which of them are generated, belongs to that Tool’s adapter. Securing what the agent may do at all is agent-permissions.

95.title: Two kinds of file, two writers
95.content: | kind | examples | source of truth | who writes the .claude/ file | . | projection (generated) | .claude/commands/<name>.md carrying a generated: key (skill:commands); the marked region of .claude/agent-memory/<agent>/MEMORY.md (agent-memory); .claude/agents/* where the memory assembler writes them; .claude/skills/ synced from packages | the skill’s front matter, the memory nodes under memory/, the package | CI only. A workflow step runs the generator and commits the result to the PR branch. | . | hand-edited | .claude/settings.json and its hooks, a hand-written command (no generated: key), an agent definition’s hand-written body, a memory file’s ## Session log | the file itself | an agent, only with the owner’s consent to that exact change | . The rule for a projection: edit the source, not the projection. To change a slash command, change the skill’s user_invocable or description. To change what a subagent remembers, add or edit a node under memory/ (agent-memory). Push the source change and let CI write the projection. You may run a generator locally in its --check form, or into a scratch tree, to see what it would write. Do not stage or commit anything it writes under .claude/. This applies inside skill-registration too. skill:register runs skill:commands, which writes .claude/commands/ in a composed checkout. Commit what it writes everywhere else, and leave .claude/ to CI. Why CI and not the agent. A projection is correct only if it was generated from the tree that lands. An agent’s local run reflects the tree it had, and a hand-merged projection drifts from its source; the CI step runs on the PR head, so the projection on the branch is the one the merge will carry, from one writer.

96.title: Hand-edited files: consent per change
96.content: Before you write a hand-edited .claude/ file: . | Show the exact diff. Paste the unified diff itself, not a description of it. | Give the reason: what breaks or is missing without the change, and what the change does to every later session (a hook that runs on every tool call; a permission that stops a prompt). | Ask, and wait. The order is context, diff, recommendation, question (interaction-modality §4.1). “Go ahead” discharges this question, for this diff only. | Record the consent in the commit that makes the change, and as a comment on the PR: . claude-config-consent: by: <owner's login> on: <ISO-8601 date-time> file: .claude/settings.json diff: <sha256 of the diff shown> evidence: "<the owner's words, verbatim>" (<session link or comment permalink>) . | . A standing waiver does not reach this. Consent is per change, so there is no gate class for it in confirmation-waiver’s table, and a waiver that claims one is not a waiver. A broad instruction such as “fix the hooks” or “make the session start work” authorises the investigation. It does not authorise the edit. Bring the diff back. When a hook or setting gets in your way, report it; do not edit it. This is the same rule as prepare-merge §Guardrails (“fix the tool” rather than delete the branch), with one extra step: here, fixing the tool is itself a change that needs consent.

97.title: Where it sits in the process
97.content: merge-to-main.bpmn runs Task_RegenProjections in its build-pipeline lane before it reads any evidence. CI regenerates the projections on the head and commits them to the PR branch, and the evidence is then read on that new head. A PR whose projections are stale therefore cannot reach the merge gate looking green (merge-to-main (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)).

1703.content: Measured from folio-assistant-core/translations, that instance's own translation-sources directory. Scroll horizontally to see all columns → . | locale | catalogues / templatesQ1: availability | entriesQ2: strings | translated | fuzzy | untranslated | officialQ3: signed off | . | ar Arabic | 6 / 3815.8% · view files → | 361 | 361100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | es Spanish | 6 / 3815.8% · view files → | 346 | 346100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | fr French | 6 / 3815.8% · view files → | 346 | 346100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | ru Russian | 6 / 3815.8% · view files → | 346 | 346100% | 0 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . | zh Chinese | 6 / 3815.8% · view files → | 361 | 35999.4% | 2 | 0 | not signed off (machine or agent translation) | . Two questions, not one. catalogues / templates asks whether a .po exists at all for each extractable .pot; the string columns ask how much of the catalogues that DO exist is done. A locale can be near 100% translated across a handful of catalogues while most of its templates have none — which is why the first column is not folded into the rest. “no basis” is not zero. A share over an empty denominator is undefined, and rendering it as 0% would report a measurement this run did not make. One directory per table, each named. translation-sources is a graph KIND, and more than one instance may declare it; the first table measures the directory named in the subtitle, and each instance below it gets its own table for its own declared directory. They are never summed: two instances' catalogues answer two questions. A catalogue sitting in an instance that has not declared the directory is invisible here — which is a gap in that declaration rather than a locale with no work done, and the two must not read the same. Fuzzy is counted apart from translated. A fuzzy entry has a translation and needs review; adding it to translated would flatter exactly the entries a reviewer must look at.

1732.title: WHO publication design (Western Pacific Region)
1732.content: who-publication-design · shipped by who-iris · skills/voices/who-publication-design · every who-iris voice . IRI: https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/who-iris/voice/who-publication-design · JSON-LD . The visual conventions around the prose rather than the prose itself: logo use, palette, typography, pagination and figure accessibility, as set out in the WHO Western Pacific Region publication and information products style guide. This is the one voice whose rules mostly do not touch a block's text, which is why it is a separate voice rather than more rules on who-editorial — a folio can want WHO's editorial register without WPRO's brand. 8 rule(s) · overlay voice-overlay-who-publication-design at major · provenance assertion · derived from Publication and Information Products Style Guide (2020) . | rule | what it asks | category · severity | the passage it was read from | . | who-des-figure-colour-accessibility | Never red with green, never blue with yellowThe guide's one hard accessibility rule for figures, and the one that matters most for a generated chart: do not combine red and green, and do not combine blue and yellow. Both pairs are the classic confusion axes. It points onward to "Accessible Publishing at WHO" for the rest. Note this agrees with this repo's own `dataviz` skill and `docs/accessibility.md`, so a folio activating this voice is not taking on a conflicting rule. | accessibility · critical | • Recommended font size 10pts • Avoid combining red and green. Avoid combining blue and yellow. For further information please check "Accessible Publishing at WHO"wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng#page-020, p18 | . | who-des-figure-font-size | 10pt in graphs, figures and tablesThe recommended font size inside a figure or a table is 10pt. Stated on both the figure page and the table page, so it is the guide's setting for data presentation generally rather than a one-off. | formatting · minor | Graphs and figures sample • Recommended font size 10pts … Table sample • Recommended font size 10ptswpr-rdo-2020-003-eng#page-020, p18, 19 | . | who-des-pagination-roman-then-arabic | Roman numerals for the front matter, Arabic for the bodyPreliminary pages take lower-case Roman numerals and the body takes Arabic. The guide also fixes the order of the front matter: title page; copyright, disclaimer and cataloguing behind the title page; table of contents listing chapters, figures and tables; foreword or preface; acknowledgements; list of contributors; list of abbreviations; executive summary. Then the body: chapters, references or bibliography, annexes. | structure · minor | PAGINATION Preliminary pages have lower-case Roman page numbers • Title page • Copyright + disclaimer + cataloging (behind title page) • (list of chapters, figures and tables) • Foreword or Preface • Acknowledgments • List of contributors • List of abbreviations • Executive summary Main pages have Arabic page numbers • Chapters • References or bibliography • Annexeswpr-rdo-2020-003-eng#page-023, p21 | . | who-des-logo-integrity | The logo is placed, never redrawnDo not alter, rotate or modify the logo, never recreate it, and do not obstruct it. Three versions exist — blue, black, and white on a dark background — and the logo may only appear on materials WPRO has endorsed. That last clause is a permission, not a style preference: a folio that is not a WPRO product must not carry it at all. | visual-identity · critical | The logo for the World Health Organization Regional Office for the Western Pacific (WPRO) should only be used on materials endorsed by WPRO. It should be presented as per guidelines here. This is essential to maintain a consistent presentation of our identity. Do not alter, rotate or modify the logo. It should never be recreated. Do not obstruct the logo. Three versions: The three versions of the WPRO logo are Blue, Black and White on a dark backgroundwpr-rdo-2020-003-eng#page-006, p4 | . | who-des-logo-exclusion-zone | 1 cm of clear space, 3 cm minimum sizeLeave an exclusion zone of at least 1 cm on every side of the logo, equal on all sides, and never reproduce it below 3 cm — the guide's stated floor for legibility in print and on screen. Where it sits beside another logo the clear space is no less than a quarter of the logo's width. | visual-identity · major | Leave "exclusion zones" around the logos (at least 1cm width distance) around the logos to ensure they maintain visual impact. Also the minimum logo size is 3cm (the smallest size at which the logo is still legible in print and on screen) For other sizes, no less than 1/4 width of logo. … Clear space should be equal on all sides.wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng#page-007, p5-6 | . | who-des-brand-blue | The regional blue is C95 M25 Y0 K0 / R0 G147 B213The primary logo blue, given in both CMYK and RGB. A folio reproducing the brand takes the values from the guide rather than sampling them from an image — a sampled colour is a colour that drifted. | visual-identity · minor | C: 95 M: 25 Y: 0 K:0 / R: 0 G: 147 B: 213 / C: 0 M: 0 Y: 0 K: 100wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng#page-006, p4 | . | who-des-typeface-family | One of four typefaces, for brand recognition rather than tasteNews Gothic MT, DIN OT, PT Sans or Calibri, each with its stated weights; Times New Roman appears with a sample as well. The guide's reason is family resemblance across WHO products, which is why it is a rule rather than a suggestion, and why substituting a similar-looking font defeats it. Body samples are set at 10pt with leading of 12–13pt. | formatting · minor | Consistent fonts across our communications help brand recognition. This helps people recognize WHO publications and communications as part of the same family and gives our products a professional look and feel. News Gothic MT (bold, regular, italic) • DIN OT (bold, medium, regular, italic, condense, condense medium, light, light italic) PT Sans (bold, regular, italic, narrow, narrow regular) • Calibri (bold, regular, italic, light italic, light)wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng#page-014, p12-13 | . | who-des-photo-provenance | Prefer WHO images, and credit themPhotographs should come from the Regional Office or the WHO photo library where possible, and carry credits. A folio's figure with no credit line is the finding here — the same provenance discipline the rest of this platform applies to a measurement or a quotation. | visual-identity · minor | Photos and credits It is best to use WHO images from the Regional Office or WHO photo librarywpr-rdo-2020-003-eng#page-026, p24 | .

1734.title: WHO guideline development
1734.content: who-guideline-development · shipped by who-iris · skills/voices/who-guideline-development · every who-iris voice . IRI: https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/who-iris/voice/who-guideline-development · JSON-LD . How a WHO recommendation is worded and what must travel with it: strength, certainty, justification, remarks and a link to the evidence. Derived from the WHO handbook for guideline development, 2nd edition. This voice governs the language of normative statements, not the process that produces them — the process is the handbook's subject and belongs in a workflow, not a style rule. 8 rule(s) · overlay voice-overlay-who-guideline-development at critical · provenance assertion · derived from WHO handbook for guideline development, 2nd ed. (2014) . | rule | what it asks | category · severity | the passage it was read from | . | who-gdl-strength-verbs | "should" is strong; "suggest" or "consider" is conditionalGRADE's wording convention, adopted by the handbook: a strong recommendation uses "should" or "strongly recommend"; a conditional one uses "suggest" or "consider". The two vocabularies must not be mixed, because the verb is how a reader learns the strength — a conditional recommendation phrased with "should" reads as strong and will be implemented as one. | methodology · critical | GRADE recommends using terms or phrases such as "should" or "strongly recommend" for strong recommendations, and "suggest" or "consider" for conditional ones.9789241548960-eng#sec-180-106-writing-recommendations, p131 | . | who-gdl-no-not-recommended | Never "not recommended" — say "we recommend against X"The handbook singles this phrase out as ambiguous, and names both readings: it can mean that no recommendation either way was made, or that the intervention should not be implemented. Where the second is meant, the required wording is "we recommend against intervention X…". This is the one rule in the voice whose severity is about reader safety rather than register: the two readings lead to opposite clinical actions. | methodology · critical | The use of confusing or ambiguous phrases should be avoided. For example, the phrase "not recommended" could be interpreted to mean either that no recommendation for or against the intervention has been made, or that the intervention should not be implemented. In the latter instance, "we recommend against intervention X…" is the preferred wording.9789241548960-eng#sec-180-106-writing-recommendations, p131 | . | who-gdl-active-voice | Recommendations are written in the active voice, and worded consistentlyThe handbook asks for the active voice and for consistency across every recommendation in one guideline. Consistency is the harder half and the one a per-block check cannot see: it is a property of the set, so a reviewer must read the recommendations together rather than one at a time. | register · major | The language of each recommendation is critically important. Wherever possible, it should be consistent across all recommendations in a guideline, which should be written in the active voice.9789241548960-eng#sec-180-106-writing-recommendations, p131 | . | who-gdl-no-outcomes-in-the-statement | Keep outcomes out of the recommendation itselfNaming an outcome in the recommendation implies that outcome was the only one considered. The handbook asks that outcomes generally stay out of the statement — they belong in the evidence summary and the remarks. A recommendation that reads "…to reduce mortality" is the shape to question. | structure · major | Outcomes should generally not be mentioned in the recommendation to avoid the impression that only single outcomes are relevant or were considered.9789241548960-eng#sec-180-106-writing-recommendations, p131 | . | who-gdl-pico-and-actionable | Clear, actionable, and in PICO shapeA recommendation reflects the PICO format — population, intervention, comparator, outcome — and is actionable: a reader must be able to tell who it applies to and what to do. Combined with the rule above, the resolution is that P, I and C appear in the statement while O informs it without being named. | structure · major | Recommendations need to be clear and actionable, reflect the PICO format and contain an indication of their strength and of the quality of the evidence on which they are based.9789241548960-eng#sec-180-106-writing-recommendations, p131 | . | who-gdl-certainty-four-levels | State the certainty as high, moderate, low or very lowFour levels, named exactly. A recommendation with no stated certainty is incomplete, and so is one that grades the evidence on some other scale — "strong evidence" is not a GRADE level and conflates certainty with strength, which the handbook keeps apart throughout. | methodology · major | The quality of the underlying body of evidence (high, moderate, low or very low) should be specified.9789241548960-eng#sec-180-106-writing-recommendations, p131 | . | who-gdl-justification-and-remarks | Every recommendation carries its justification, its remarks and a link to the evidenceFour things travel with the statement: why it is strong or conditional, why it is for or against, remarks giving the conditions and context in which it applies and what to bear in mind when implementing it, and a link to the evidence — a systematic review, the GRADE evidence profiles and the evidence-to-decision tables. A block carrying the recommendation and none of these is not yet a recommendation; in a folio this is what `uses[]` and the evidence sidecar are for. | structure · major | A recommendation should include a justification as to why it is strong or conditional and why it is for or against a given intervention. It should also contain a set of remarks explaining the conditions and context in which the recommendation applies and the points to bear in mind regarding implementation. … Each recommendation should be linked to a summary of the evidence (e.g. a published systematic review or the systematic review in an online annex), the GRADE evidence profiles and the evidence-to-decision tables.9789241548960-eng#sec-180-106-writing-recommendations, p131-132 | . | who-gdl-conditional-states-its-conditions | A conditional recommendation names the conditionsThe handbook's account of why a recommendation is conditional — the GDG being less certain about the balance of benefits against harms — carries a drafting consequence: a conditional recommendation generally includes a description of the conditions under which the end-user should or should not implement it. So "we suggest X" with no conditions attached has the form of a conditional recommendation and not the content. | structure · major | Recommendations that are conditional or weak are made when a GDG is less certain about the balance between the benefits and harms or disadvantages of implementing a recommendation. Conditional recommendations generally include a description of the conditions under which the end-user should or should not implement the recommendation.9789241548960-eng#sec-177-1042-conditional-or-weak-recommendations, p129 | .

1736.title: WHO editorial style
1736.content: who-editorial · shipped by who-iris · skills/voices/who-editorial · every who-iris voice . IRI: https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/who-iris/voice/who-editorial · JSON-LD . The house editorial style of the World Health Organization: spelling, capitalization, eponym form, reference layout and non-discriminatory language, as set out in the WHO Editorial Style Manual. Derived rule by rule from the ingested manual; every rule cites the page it was read from. 25 rule(s) · overlay voice-overlay-who-editorial at major · provenance assertion · derived from WHO Editorial Style Manual (1993) . | rule | what it asks | category · severity | the passage it was read from | . | who-ed-ize-preferred | -ize, not -iseWhere a word may be spelled with -ize or -ise, use -ize: organize, not organise; organization, not organisation. The manual's stated ground is the Greek root and the first spelling in The concise Oxford dictionary. The exception is a word where -ise is not a suffix but part of the root — surprise, comprise, improvise — which keep -ise. This rule is the reason the voice had to be derived rather than assumed: it is commonly believed that WHO house style is -ise, and PR #210 asserted exactly that. | spelling · major | Where there is a choice between using the suffix -ize or -ise (e.g. organize or organise), -ize, derived from the Greek "-izo", is preferred, consistent with the first spelling of such words given in The concise Oxford dictionary. For some words, such as surprise, comprise or improvise, where -ise is not a suffix but part of the root of the word, there is no choice.who-pub-tps-931#page-014, p14 | . | who-ed-eponym-no-genitive | Crohn disease, not Crohn's diseaseAn eponymous name takes no Saxon genitive: Crohn disease, Down syndrome. The manual goes further and asks that eponyms be avoided altogether where a descriptive name exists, on the ground that an eponym carries no information about the disease and may name something different in another country — so a finding here is worth reading as two questions, not one. | terminology · major | Eponymous names give no information about the nature of the disease and different names may be used in different countries. They should be avoided whenever possible. The Saxon genitive ('s) is not necessary when using an eponymous name; e.g. Crohn disease, not Crohn's disease, and Down syndrome, not Down's syndrome.who-pub-tps-931#page-009, p9 | . | who-ed-who-capitalization | Member State, the Organization — and headquarters, primary health careThe manual gives two explicit lists rather than a principle, and the two halves are easy to get backwards. Capitalised: Member State, Associate Member, the Organization (meaning WHO), the Constitution, Region in a specific reference, Regional Committee, Regional Director, World Health Assembly, General Programme of Work, Global Strategy for Health for All. Lower case: headquarters, primary health care, health for all, session, resolution, decision, strategy, specialized agency, representatives, committee and commission unless specifically identified, region used generically, and names of seasons. Note the pair the manual calls out itself: member (of a committee) but Member (State). | capitalization · minor | The following words and expressions used frequently within WHO normally require capitalization: Associate Member; Constitution (of WHO); (Eighth) General Programme of Work; Forty-… World Health Assembly; … Member (country); Member State; … the Organization (WHO); Region [of WHO] … / The following words and expressions do not normally require capitalization: commission, committee (unless specifically identified); … health for all; headquarters (WHO); member (of the committee, etc.), but Member (State); … primary health care; … specialized agencywho-pub-tps-931#page-013, p13-14 | . | who-ed-capitals-sparingly | Capitals break the eye; use them for names, not for importanceProper names, titles and institutions take capitals. Descriptive appellations — administrative posts and the like — do not, unless lower case would read oddly. A trade name takes an initial capital (Pyrex, Vaseline, with the generic preferred where one exists); a Linnaean genus takes one (Staphylococcus aureus, Trypanosoma) while the anglicised common form does not (trypanosome, schistosome). Article, book and journal titles in references are NOT capitalised except where they contain an organization's name. | capitalization · minor | Too many capital letters break the flow of the eye across a sentence and down a column of type. However, proper names, titles and institutions require capitals. Descriptive appellations, such as administrative posts, do not, unless the result would appear odd or confusing. … Generic terms in the Linnaean classification also take an initial capital letter, e.g. Staphylococcus aureus, Trypanosoma, Schistosoma, but trypanosome, schistosome, etc. Article, book and journal titles in references need not be capitalized, e.g. Social science and medicine, except when they contain the name of an association or organizationwho-pub-tps-931#page-013, p13 | . | who-ed-reference-authors | All authors up to three; et al. from fourList every author when there are three or fewer. From four, give the first author only and add et al. Author names are surname followed by initials with no periods and no comma between them — Cairns RB, DuPont B, Crompton DWT et al. | citation · major | 1. List all authors when three or fewer; when four or more, give only first author's name and add et al.who-pub-tps-931#page-033, p33 | . | who-ed-journal-names-in-full | Write journal names out in fullNo abbreviated journal titles. The manual's reason is worth keeping with the rule, because it decides the borderline cases: it is for readers whose first language is not English, who cannot expand an unfamiliar abbreviation. So 'Bulletin of the World Health Organization', never 'Bull World Health Organ'. | citation · major | 2. Write out journal names in full. This is particularly helpful to readers whose mother tongue is not English.who-pub-tps-931#page-033, p33 | . | who-ed-non-discriminatory-language | Rewrite, do not decorate: the non-discriminatory pairsThe manual's own table, which is prescriptive about the TECHNIQUE and not only the vocabulary. Its four general rules are: delete redundant possessive pronouns; rephrase; use the first person plural; and use neutral or equivalent job titles. Its worked substitutions include foreman/workman/office girl/policeman becoming supervisor/worker/secretary or receptionist or office assistant/police officer; 'Man, mankind' and 'the average man' rephrased; 'show the mother how to cook' becoming 'show members of the family', on the stated ground that women are not assumed to do the household chores; 'ask mothers to bring their children' becoming 'ask parents', because men have responsibility for children too; and 'Mrs John Smith' becoming 'Jane Smith'. | terminology · major | Common discriminatory phrases / Useful solutions / Useful general rules … Delete redundant possessive pronouns … Use the first person plural … Foreman, workman, office girl, policeman → Supervisor, worker, secretary, receptionist, office assistant, police officer → Use neutral or equivalent job titles … Show the mother how to cook nutritious meals → Show members of the family how to cook nutritious meals → Do not assume that women always do the household chores … Ask mothers to bring their children to the clinic each month → Ask parents to bring their children to the clinic each month → Remember that men have responsibility for children toowho-pub-tps-931#page-070, p70-72 | . | who-ed-rewriting-stays-concise | The rewrite is not more cumbersome — that is the manual's own claimThe manual anticipates the objection that non-discriminatory phrasing is clumsy and answers it with worked pairs of equal length, moving to the plural rather than to 'he or she': 'He may see himself as the pivot of all that happens … may comment on the patient or address him' becomes 'Patients may see themselves as the pivot of all that happens … may comment on or address patients'. So a reviewer should reject 'he or she' and 's/he' patches and ask for the plural or a rephrase. It also asks that research involving both sexes report both, and that gross figures in statistical reports be broken down by sex unless no significant difference has already been established. | register · minor | With care, the results of rewriting text to eliminate discriminatory language will be no less concise than the original — but will be unambiguous and will avoid causing offence. … In reporting research of any kind that involves both men and women and/or children of both sexes, both males and females should be mentioned in the results. In statistical reports, gross figures should be broken down by sex unless it has previously been established that there is no significant difference between the sexes.who-pub-tps-931#page-069, p69 | . | who-ed-country-names-are-volatile | Country names are checked, not rememberedThe manual is explicit that country names and their spellings change 'at an alarming rate' and names the office that holds the current list, with full, short and adjectival forms. The rule for an author or an agent is therefore procedural: do not spell a Member State's name from memory or from an older document in the same corpus. This is judgement-only by construction — no pattern can know which name was current when a passage was written. | terminology · minor | Webster's new geographical dictionary … can be used as a guide to the spelling of common geographical entities. However, country names and their spelling, in particular, can change at an alarming rate. The Computer-Assisted Translation and Terminology subunit (CTT), which coordinates with the Office of the Legal Counsel (LEG), can provide up-to-date information on the names of United Nations and WHO Member States, including their full, short and adjectival/attributive forms.who-pub-tps-931#page-009, p9 | . | who-ed-spelling-general | Follow The concise Oxford dictionary's first spelling — and Annex 1 where WHO differsThe general spelling rule the manual's Annex 1 opens with: take the spelling The concise Oxford dictionary gives first, or the one a variant entry refers you to. Annex 1 then lists WHO's own exceptions and the words that most often cause doubt; the rules who-ed-spelling-annex-p088 to p102 carry that list, one rule per printed page, each quoting its page. Where a word is not listed, this rule decides. | spelling · minor | The general rule in WHO is to follow the spelling given in the latest edition of The concise Oxford dictionary; where it gives alternative spellings or forms, use the one given first (e.g. fulfil, fulfill) or the one to which you are referred from an entry giving a variant spelling (e.g. "tire, US var. of tyre": use "tyre").who-pub-tps-931#page-088, p88 | . | who-ed-spelling-annex-p088 | Annex 1 spellings, printed page 83The entries on printed page 83 of Annex 1 ("Spelling of words that commonly cause difficulty") that name a form to avoid — marked by an italic not, or by prefer, avoid, use or deprecated. 1741.content: agent-skill-authoring-gemini-cli · shipped by cat-harness · cat-harness/skills/voices/vendors/agent-skill-authoring-gemini-cli · every cat-harness voice . IRI: https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant/cat-harness/voice/agent-skill-authoring-gemini-cli · JSON-LD . What Gemini CLI's own documentation adds to the shared base voice (agent-skill-authoring): its loading budget in words, its degrees-of-freedom rule, its folder names, script ergonomics and security. MODEL-SPECIFIC by the owner's ruling (bean rkqp, 2026-09-20): a vendor's advice is evidence about that vendor's platform, so it is a separate voice extending the base rather than caveats folded into it — a rule that turns out to be Gemini-only can then be dropped without touching the rest. Provenance is ASSERTION: a publisher describing its own product, revisable without notice. Rules the base already states (description carries function and trigger; read third-party skills before installing) are inherited through extends, not repeated. Conformance is an agentic review, never a schema gate — the owner's instruction, because 'best practice' drifts. 10 rule(s) · overlay voice-overlay-agent-skill-authoring-gemini-cli at major · provenance assertion · derived from Agent Skill best practices | Gemini CLI (captured 2026-09-20, page last updated 2026-04-30) (2026) . | rule | what it asks | category · severity | the passage it was read from | . | gc-descriptions-do-not-overlap | A description is distinct from every other skill's — and from what the model does anywayGemini CLI routes on the description alone, so two skills whose descriptions cover the same requests compete for them, and a description that restates a general capability of the model gives the router no reason to load the skill at all. Check a new description against the descriptions already installed, not only against the skill's own body. | structure · major | Avoid overlap: Ensure your skill descriptions are distinct from one another and from the general capabilities of the model.agent-skill-best-practices---gemini-cli#page-001, p1 | . | gc-context-budget-in-words | Budget the three loading levels in WORDS: ~100 always loaded, under 5k on triggerGemini CLI states its budget per level and in words: the name and description are always in context (~100 words), the SKILL.md body is loaded only when the skill triggers (under 5,000 words), and bundled resources only as needed. The base voice's '~500 lines' comes from a different source and a different unit; on Gemini CLI the word budget is the vendor's own figure. Neither is a hard limit the platform enforces — both are the publisher's guidance. | numbers · minor | 1. Metadata (name + description): Always in context (~100 words). 2. SKILL.md body: Loaded only after the skill triggers (<5k words). 3. Bundled resources: Loaded only as needed by the model.agent-skill-best-practices---gemini-cli#page-001, p1 | . | gc-degrees-of-freedom | Match how prescriptive a step is to how fragile it isThree levels: text instructions where several approaches are valid, pseudocode or a parameterised script where one pattern is preferred, and a specific script with few parameters where the operation is fragile or the sequence MUST be followed. Writing a fragile step as free prose is the failure this prevents; so is scripting a judgement call. | methodology · major | Degrees of freedom Match the level of instruction specificity to the task’s fragility. High freedom (text-based instructions): Use when multiple approaches are valid or decisions depend heavily on context. Medium freedom (pseudocode or scripts with parameters): Use when a preferred pattern exists but some variation is acceptable. Low freedom (specific scripts, few parameters): Use when operations are fragile and error-prone, or a specific sequence MUST be followed.agent-skill-best-practices---gemini-cli#page-002, p2 | . | gc-scripts-for-deterministic-tasks | A task a script can do is a script in scripts/, not proseIf the step is deterministic — run a linter, fetch from an API — bundle it as a script under scripts/ and have the body call it, rather than describing the commands for the model to reproduce each time. | structure · minor | Use scripts for deterministic tasks: If a task can be automated with a script (for example, running a linter, fetching data from an API), bundle it in the scripts/ folder.agent-skill-best-practices---gemini-cli#page-002, p2 | . | gc-llm-friendly-script-output | A bundled script's output is written for a model to readSuppress verbose tracebacks and end with a clear, short success or failure message. The reader of a skill script's stdout is the agent, and a stack trace is context it pays for without learning what to do next. | formatting · minor | Agentic ergonomics: Ensure scripts output LLM-friendly stdout. Suppress verbose tracebacks and provide clear, concise success/failure messages.agent-skill-best-practices---gemini-cli#page-002, p2 | . | gc-templates-in-assets | Boilerplate the agent must reproduce exactly lives in assets/Common file headers and boilerplate go in assets/ as templates, so every run produces the same output rather than the model's recollection of it. | structure · minor | Provide templates: Include common file headers or boilerplate code in the assets/ folder to ensure the agent produces consistent output.agent-skill-best-practices---gemini-cli#page-002, p2 | . | gc-skill-directory-anatomy | SKILL.md is required; scripts/, references/ and assets/ are the optional sub-foldersGemini CLI's layout: SKILL.md (core instructions and metadata) is the only required file; executable logic goes in scripts/, documentation loaded on demand in references/, templates and other non-executable resources in assets/. Other vendors name these folders differently — Antigravity documents examples/ and resources/ — which is why this is a vendor rule and not a base one. | structure · minor | my-skill/ ├── SKILL.md (Required) Core instructions and metadata ├── scripts/ (Optional) Executable logic (Node.js, Python, etc.) ├── references/ (Optional) Documentation to be loaded as needed └── assets/ (Optional) Templates and non-executable resourcesagent-skill-best-practices---gemini-cli#page-002, p2 | . | gc-reference-material-out-of-the-body | Keep the body procedural; reference material, schemas and examples go in references/The body holds the core procedure. Detailed reference material, schemas and examples move to separate files in references/, loaded only when needed — the vendor's own folder name for what the base voice calls a reference file. | structure · minor | Best practice: Keep the SKILL.md body focused on core procedural instructions. Move detailed reference material, schemas, and examples into separate files in a references/ directory.agent-skill-best-practices---gemini-cli#page-002, p2 | . | gc-no-hardcoded-secrets | No API key or password in a skill's scripts or documentationA skill is shared and installed by others; a credential written into it is published with it. | methodology · critical | Avoid hardcoded secrets: Never include API keys or passwords in your skill’s scripts or documentation.agent-skill-best-practices---gemini-cli#page-003, p3 | . | gc-limit-scope | Keep a skill as narrow as it can beThe narrower the skill, the smaller the damage when it is wrong. A skill that does several things fails in several places at once. | structure · minor | Limit scope: Design skills to be as focused as possible to minimize the potential impact of errors.agent-skill-best-practices---gemini-cli#page-003, p3 | .
