If data are not available for practising or professionally active health workers, data with the closest definition can be used, such as “health worker licensed to practice”. Categories of level are based on the definitions of OECD/Eurostat/WHO-Europe Joint questionnaire on non-monetary health care statistics. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 88; PDF page 102). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. A job is defined as “a set of tasks and duties performed, or meant to be performed, by one person, including for an employer or in self-employment”. The National Health Workforce Accounts covers health and health-related occupations grouped according to the International Standard Classification of Occupations 2008. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). The library ingest of this edition has no Glossary section, so the definition was extracted from the PDF text layer on 2026-10-31 and needs a person to confirm it. The handbook cites its reference 46 for this entry. | Remuneration (National health workforce accounts: a handbook, second edition (2023))Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. It should be net of operation costs/practice expenses. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). As a social construct, gender varies from society to society and can change over time. Gender is hierarchical and produces inequalities that intersect with other social and economic inequalities. Outcome indicators candidate Indicators that provide insights into the tangible results for stakeholders that arise from the adoption and use of eHealth. Worldwide, the application of information and communication technologies to support national health-care services is rapidly expanding and increasingly important. This is especially so at a time when all health systems face stringent economic challenges and greater demands to provide more and better care, especially to those most in need. The National eHealth Strategy Toolkit is an expert, practical guide that provides governments, their ministries and stakeholders with a solid foundation and method for the development and implementation of a national eHealth vision, action plan and monitoring framework. All countries, whatever their level of development, can adapt the Toolkit to suit their own circumstances. Representing one of the most significant collaborations in recent years between the World Health Organization and the International Telecommunication Union, the Toolkit is a landmark in understanding what eHealth is, what it can do, and why and how it should be applied to health care today. Public Health Workforce candidate The public health workforce comprises all individuals who contribute to the delivery of at least one of the essential public health functions as part of integrated services and systems. This workforce comprises diverse and multidisciplinary occupations, from the health as well as other non-health sectors. This workforce can be conceptualized as three broad groupings: core group of public health personnel who have undergone professional training and/or registration with professional bodies in public health and could be from either health or another background; health and care workers who contribute to one or more public health functions as part of their clinical and/or social care roles; and personnel from a wide group of other allied occupations who contribute to addressing the determinants of health – for instance, personnel engaged in water and sanitation, food supply chains and road safety. 3528.content: quality assurance QA candidate No definition yet. Verbatim from the source; a candidate until an editor adopts it (glossary-from-source). Term page · Digital transformation handbook for health supply chain architecture · https://worldhealthorganization.github.io/who-iris/v0/ns/glossary/9789240101197-eng/quality-assurance · source library/9789240101197-eng/sections/sec-001-abbreviations-and-acronyms.md#L48 . quality of the evidence In the context of guideline development, the confidence that the estimates of an effect are adequate to support a particular decision or recommendation. Rated high, moderate, low or very low. The WHO handbook for guideline development (2nd edition, §9.1, p. 122) names both alternatives: "Alternative terms to describe the quality of the evidence are 'certainty of the evidence' or 'confidence in the estimates of effect'." The handbook uses 'quality of the evidence' 77 times and 'certainty of the evidence' once; the who-guideline-development voice and the platform's `grade-certainty` code list use 'certainty', GRADE's later name. Rated for a body of evidence per outcome, never for a single study. Not the strength of a recommendation, which the handbook keeps apart throughout. Remuneration candidate Average gross annual income earned by employees or those self-employed, i.e. income per year and per person, before any deductions are made for social security contributions or income tax. A person may have more than one qualifying job in any given reference period. • Income earned by employees (earnings) refers to all payments – in cash or in kind, for work done or time worked – made by their employers, and includes basic wages, overtime and other bonuses (such as for night work, work on weekends), all allowances paid by the employer (such as for working away from home or for housing) and all commissions and gratuities paid by the employer. Employers may be the government, corporations, non-profit institutions or households. • Income earned by self-employed workers refers to all payments, in cash or in kind, made by customers for goods or services, and includes capitation or fee-for-service reimbursement, bonuses, commissions, and gratuities. It should be net of operation costs/practice expenses. From the Glossary of the handbook (p. 92; PDF page 106). 3548.title: Already somebody else’s concept?
3548.content: Extracted candidates are minted from this repository’s own assets and are not, by themselves, checked against any vocabulary. check:term-mapping asks whether each already exists as a concept somebody is authoritative for — SKOS for what a term MEANS, FHIR for a clinical code’s operational semantics — and the two are separate questions with separate answers. Already somebody else's concept? — check:term-mapping, bean 7wou | target | mapped | unmapped | undetermined | why undetermined | . | fhir | 0 | 327 | 0 | — | . | skos | 0 | 327 | 0 | — | . Undetermined is never “no match”. A vocabulary that could not be reached has said nothing, and the column above keeps that apart from a checked miss. The counts are reported and not graded: an unmapped candidate may be a term this corpus is right to coin.

3584.title: What a folio is
3584.content: The knowledge graph is four sub-graphs, and a layer declares which of them it holds. Content is what somebody authors and a reader reads — this layer’s subject. Skills are the instructions an agent follows to do the work. Processes are the BPMN diagrams that say who does what, in which order, and where the gates are — they are executable, not illustrations. Tools are what an agent can call. Getting anything in is acquisition: unstructured and semi-structured sources arrive through uploads/ or through the conversation, and are ingested into library/. It is a step rather than a graph typology of its own — there is no fifth directory to look for. Scope: the content model — what a folio IS. Not the skills and tools that operate on it, and not any particular folio’s chapters. | Content A document is structured prose; a paper adds the block kinds whose assertion is a formal claim. | Skills Every skill and role, and how they fit together. | Processes The BPMN diagrams, which are the source of truth rather than a picture of it. | Tools What an agent can call, served over MCP. | Acquisition How a source gets from uploads/ into library/. | RTFM — folio-assist-core Its scope, in and out, and why it declares no directories yet. | .

3590.title: The IRIS CDN Exporter
3590.content: Skill iris-cdn-exporter: The IRIS CDN Exporter agent — how WHO IRIS is exported onto Cloudflare — a git repository on Cloudflare Artifacts and R2 behind the CDN — with an initial load (metadata and PDFs), a nightly change ingest over the DSpace REST API, a weekly reconciliation, and one signed release per run. What the agent decides, what the pipeline does, and the no-churn rule both obey. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . The exporter is an agent role plus a set of deterministic scripts. The scripts (scripts/iris-cdn/) move bytes. The agent plans, reviews and reports. It never holds the signing key and never pushes to a WHO repository. Processes, all in processes/: . | Process | When | What | . | iris-cdn-initial-load.bpmn | once, run by hand with a stated budget | every record and every bitstream, in resumable batches | . | iris-cdn-nightly.bpmn | every night, 02:00 UTC | only the items IRIS reports as changed | . | iris-cdn-reconcile.bpmn | Sundays, 04:00 UTC | catches withdrawals, which REST does not report, and checks for drift | . | iris-cdn-sign-publish.bpmn | called by the three above | BagIt bag, detached JWS (ES256), did:web key, verify | . What each process does is in docs/iris-cdn-export.md; where it runs, what it writes where, and its secrets are in docs/iris-cdn-deployment.md; signing is skill iris-cdn-signing; reading changes from IRIS is skill iris-rest-feed.

3591.title: The no-churn rule
3591.content: Content that has not changed is not rewritten, re-uploaded or re-signed. Each step says how: . | Canonical records. A record is written as JSON with sorted keys, LF line endings and no fetch timestamp inside it. If the canonical bytes equal the held ones, the file is not rewritten. | Content-addressed bitstreams. A bitstream is stored under its SHA-256. An object that already exists is never downloaded, uploaded or overwritten again. | Sorted graph output. The graph is rebuilt in full, and N-Quads partitions are written sorted, so a partition with no changed item comes out byte-identical and is not re-uploaded. | Date-free manifests. bag-info.txt has no Bagging-Date, so the tag manifest of an unchanged payload is byte-identical. | An empty diff ends the run. No commit, no new signature. | . A step that cannot meet its rule reports it. It never hides it.

3592.title: What the agent does
3592.content: . | Plan the initial load as one batch per collection page, with the checkpoint in state/initial-load.json in the Cloudflare git repository. | Review each run report and open a bean for each anomaly: a change count far from the recent median, a quarantined bitstream, a verification whose verdict is unknown, or a partition over its size ceiling. | Never widen scope. Only the owner changes what is exported, its budget or where it is stored. | .

3593.title: What the agent must not do
3593.content: . | Push to any WHO/* repository. | Treat a short listing as a mass withdrawal (see iris-rest-feed). | Delete a published object. A withdrawn item is marked withdrawn, and its bytes stay addressable because a citation to them may exist. | Put an upstream count into prose. Counts come from the catalogue and the run reports. | .

3619.title: Signing and verifying an IRIS CDN release
3619.content: Skill iris-cdn-signing: How an IRIS CDN release is packaged, signed and verified using published standards only: a BagIt bag (RFC 8493), a detached JWS (RFC 7515 App. F) with ES256 (RFC 7518), and the key published in a did:web DID document whose publicKeyJwk carries an x5c chain up to WHO’s signing key. No GDHCN trust list is assumed. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release, Adjudicate two KG extractors, GuidelineKG nightly path: verify and adjudicate the result, GuidelineKG nightly path: prepare the work order, GuidelineKG nightly path . The code is scripts/iris-cdn/bag.ts and scripts/iris-cdn/signing.ts. The process is processes/iris-cdn-sign-publish.bpmn.

3620.title: Standards used, and nothing else
3620.content: | Piece | Standard | . | Package and digests | BagIt 1.0, RFC 8493: bagit.txt, bag-info.txt, manifest-sha256.txt, tagmanifest-sha256.txt | . | Signature | JWS compact serialization with a detached payload, RFC 7515 Appendix F | . | Algorithm | ES256, ECDSA on P-256 with SHA-256, RFC 7518 §3.4. It is the same curve as WHO’s signing DID key. EdDSA (RFC 8037) is accepted when verifying | . | Public key | JWK, RFC 7517, as publicKeyJwk | . | Trust chain | x5c in the JWK (RFC 7517 §4.7): X.509 certificates, leaf first, ending at one issued by WHO’s signing key | . | Key publication | W3C DID Core 1.0 document, verificationMethod of type JsonWebKey (W3C Controlled Identifiers 1.0) or JsonWebKey2020, which is the form WHO’s own DID uses. Both are accepted | . | DID method | did:web | . No draft standards are used. A new one needs the owner’s explicit approval.

3621.title: What is signed
3621.content: There is one release signature, over the bytes of tagmanifest-sha256.txt, plus one signature per changed library item (below). The tag manifest pins the SHA-256 of every other tag file, and manifest-sha256.txt pins the SHA-256 of every payload file. Signing the tag manifest therefore covers the whole bag. The tag files live in the release git repository; the payload files live in R2 under sha256/<aa>/<digest>. The signature is stored beside the tag manifest as tagmanifest-sha256.txt.jws, in the form <header>..<signature>. The empty middle segment is the detached payload. The protected header is {"alg":"ES256","kid":"did:web:…#<key>"}. ECDSA signatures are randomized. Signing the same bytes twice gives two different signatures, so unchanged content is never re-signed: an unchanged night produces the same tag manifest and gets no new signature.

3622.title: A signature on each library item
3622.content: Every library item has its own manifest at items/<handle>/manifest-sha256.txt, in the same line format as the BagIt payload manifest. It lists the item’s record, records/<handle>.json, and every file under bitstreams/<handle>/. The item’s detached JWS is stored beside it as manifest-sha256.txt.jws. | An item verifies on its own. Fetch its manifest and JWS, verify the JWS against the DID document and its x5c chain, then check each digest. | The release signature proves completeness. The item manifests and their JWSs are payload files, so the release tag manifest pins them all. Nothing can be added or removed without breaking the release signature. | Only changed items are signed. If an item’s manifest bytes did not change, its existing JWS is kept (signItems in scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts). A metadata-only edit changes the record digest, so that item is re-signed while its PDF digest stays the same. | .

3623.title: Where the key comes from
3623.content: The verifier resolves the kid’s DID from the web, never from the package: . | did:web:<cdn-domain> resolves to https://<cdn-domain>/.well-known/did.json, and did:web:<cdn-domain>:iris resolves to https://<cdn-domain>/iris/did.json. The DID must be stable, because the DID is the signer’s identity. | When the DID document lists assertionMethod, the key must be in it. A retired key stays in verificationMethod so that old releases still verify, but it is removed from assertionMethod. A signature by that retired key on a new release then fails. | . If the DID document cannot be fetched, the verdict is unknown, not failed and not verified. A portal that cannot check says so. The trust chain. Our key’s publicKeyJwk.x5c holds the certificates that end at one issued by the key in WHO’s signing DID, did:web:raw.githubusercontent.com:WorldHealthOrganization:tng-participants-prod:main:WHO:signing:DID. The verifier is given WHO’s public key as its anchor, as the variable IRIS_CDN_TRUST_ANCHOR_JWK in CI. With an anchor, a key with no x5c fails. run.ts verify refuses without the anchor or IRIS_CDN_DID: the verdict is unknown and it exits non-zero. Called without anchors, verifyDetached reports the chain as not-checked, never as verified. No other trust anchor is assumed. A trust list, such as GDHCN via WHO SMART Trust, could only be an additional route to the same DID document, never a replacement for it.

3624.title: Key custody and rotation
3624.content: . | The private key is a JWK (kty: EC, crv: P-256, x, y, d). It never goes into git, a log or a bean. It is the GitHub environment secret IRIS_CDN_SIGNING_JWK in environment iris-cdn-release, which only jobs on main can read. | The key already exists. The subordinate key is already published in a DID document, with x5c up to WHO’s signing DID, before the exporter runs. That publication is offline and outside these processes. No CI job issues certificates or edits the DID document. | To rotate: . | Add the new key to the DID document and to assertionMethod. | Publish the DID document. | Sign the next release with the new key. | Take the old key out of assertionMethod, and keep it in verificationMethod. | . | The DID document is built in a fixed order, so republishing it with the same keys writes the same bytes. | .

3625.title: Verifying by hand
3625.content: In a checkout of the release git repository: . # 1. tag files against the tag manifest sha256sum -c tagmanifest-sha256.txt # 2. the release signature, with the key resolved from did:web IRIS_CDN_DID=did:web:<cdn-domain> IRIS_CDN_TRUST_ANCHOR_JWK='<WHO public JWK>' \ bun scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts verify --release <checkout> --no-revert . Payload digests in manifest-sha256.txt are checked against the objects at https://<cdn-domain>/sha256/<aa>/<digest>, not against files in the checkout.

3627.title: IRIS, DSpace and Dublin Core
3627.content: Skill iris-dspace: How WHO IRIS uses DSpace and qualified Dublin Core — the three identifier systems, MeSH as a controlled vocabulary, bundles, and the containment path — and the requirements a tool reading a record must meet. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation . Every claim here is read off one captured record: the DSpace full item record for wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng, transcribed at catalogue/records/wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng.dc.json. Nothing is asserted from general knowledge of DSpace. Where this file and the record disagree, the record wins. The type is folio-assistant-core/schemas/dublin-core.ts. It is generic: Dublin Core is ISO 15836 and DSpace is a platform. This file covers only what IRIS does with them.

3628.title: Scale
3628.content: From IRIS’s storage report (By Location → Entire Site) and home page, read 2026-09-20: . |   |   | source | . | items | 273,559 | the home page’s search placeholder | . | files | 1,057,223 | the storage report | . | storage | 361.55 GB | the storage report | . | top-level communities | 8 | the storage report | . Items and files are different denominators, so catalogue/catalogue.json carries them in separate fields, totalItemsUpstream and totalFilesUpstream. That is 3.86 files per item, because an item carries several bitstreams. totalBytesUpstream is derived: the report prints two decimals and no byte count, so the value is round(361.55 × 1024³), good to about ±5 MiB. It is GiB rather than GB because every per-community figure the report prints (238.58, 19.72, 34.84, 26.14, 25.71) reproduces exactly at 2³⁰ and none does at 10⁹.

3629.title: Three identifier systems
3629.content: The worked item carries all three: . | system | value | authoritative? | . | DSpace UUID | 18892cf3-5a4f-42a4-923c-a93f4a594dec | no — IRIS’s own, stable only while this DSpace instance is | . | Handle | 10665/332098 | yes — guaranteed by the Handle System, outside WHO | . | WHO govdoc | WPR/RDO/2020/003 | no — WHO’s publication number | . The library slug wpr-rdo-2020-003-eng is derived from the govdoc, the weakest key. A tool that resolves by Handle survives the source moving. A legacy handle is live in the record, and must not be deduplicated . dc.identifier.uri appears twice: . https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/332098 ← global http://iris.wpro.who.int/handle/10665.1/14518 ← regional, merged away . Regional IRIS instances were folded into the global one and both URIs were kept. The second is a real alternate identifier, and evidence that a source host can disappear (the sourceLoss gate’s worked example).

3630.title: Qualified, repeated, language-tagged
3630.content: Every field is element.qualifier. Four fields repeat in this one record (dc.date.accessioned, dc.date.available, dc.identifier.uri, dc.subject.mesh), so Record<string, string> silently keeps the last value and drops the rest. There is a per-field language column, present on dc.title, dc.description and each dc.subject.mesh, absent on the author, the dates and the identifiers. An absent tag is not en: it is a value whose language nobody asserted.

3631.title: MeSH is a controlled vocabulary, not a keyword
3631.content: dc.subject.mesh = Publishing, Guidelines as Topic. These are NLM Medical Subject Headings, with their own identifiers and hierarchy at https://id.nlm.nih.gov/mesh/. A MeSH term can be resolved and subsumed (searching “Guidelines as Topic” should reach narrower terms); a free-text keyword can do neither. DcValue.authority records the distinction per value.

3632.title: An item is not a file: bundles
3632.content: DSpace groups bitstreams into bundles — conventionally ORIGINAL, plus TEXT (extracted), THUMBNAIL and LICENSE. Size and format are per-bitstream: the 2.68 MB in the record is the PDF’s, not the item’s. Bundles are why there are more files than items.

3633.title: Containment is a path, not a parent
3633.content: The breadcrumb: Home → 7. Regional Office for the … → Regional Office for the W… → Information products — four levels, two of them communities and one a collection. DSpace also lets an item be mapped into several collections, so “the” parent of a node does not exist. CatalogueNode.parents is a list of paths.

3634.title: What a later tool needs — as requirements
3634.content: | # | requirement | why, in one line | . | R1 | Resolve by Handle where one exists; treat UUID and govdoc as secondary | only the Handle is guaranteed outside WHO | . | R2 | Never deduplicate dc.identifier.uri | the second one is evidence of a host that vanished | . | R3 | Preserve repetition on every field, not a known list | four fields repeat in a single record; assume more do | . | R4 | Treat an absent language as unasserted, never as en | both states occur in one record | . | R5 | Carry dc.subject.mesh as a controlled value with its authority | it can be resolved and subsumed; a keyword cannot | . | R6 | Model bitstreams per bundle, with size and format on the bitstream | an item is not a file | . | R7 | Model containment as a list of paths | four levels deep, and multiple mappings are legal | . | R8 | Never infer metadata from the PDF when a record exists | OCR off a title page catalogued the WHO Editorial Style Manual as Abies | . | R9 | Record what the source says even when it contradicts the file | dc.description says 30 p.; the PDF has 33 | . | R10 | An item with no known collection carries parents: [] — never a guessed one | held-and-unplaceable is a STATE; inventing containment is unfalsifiable | . | R11 | Key a node by path when its UUID is not in the capture | an invented UUID resolves to nothing while looking authoritative | . | R12 | Keep the page captured and the identifier apart | /items/<uuid>/full is what was fetched; the Handle is what the item IS | . | R13 | A materialized claim must name bytes that EXIST, and something must check it | an unchecked claim can name no bytes and still pass as held | . | R14 | Read a storage figure in the units that round-trip its own bytes | IRIS prints “GB” for what its byte counts make GiB — a 7% error | . | R15 | Never fall back to a parent URL when an item has no upstream URI | “no upstream URI recorded” is the answer; the front page is a lie that resolves | . | R16 | A partial transcription must SAY it is partial | a truncated abstract that does not declare itself cannot be told from a short one | . | R17 | Hold what you hold: model the bitstreams whose bytes are here | the handbook lists 8 upstream; this repository has 1 | . | R18 | Do not “correct” a record that looks wrong | the English-titled editorial manual really does carry an Italian ISBN | . | R19 | A derived figure must round-trip the figure it was derived from | round(361.55 × 1024³) bytes must render back as 361.55 GiB | . | R20 | An item count and a file count are different denominators | 273,559 against 1,057,223 — a fraction built from the wrong one is off by 3.86× | . | R21 | Mint stable URIs at the extractor (Upstream Skolemization) | minting https://iris.who.int/entity/item/{handle}#{prop}_{idx} at extraction leaves no blank nodes for a later pass to resolve | . | R22 | Append-only streaming partition writes | A 300,000 item corpus cannot accumulate uncompressed in working memory; write quads directly to partition file streams | . R8: where a library entry’s title comes from . who-pub-tps-931 shows why. Its structure.json carries title: "Abies" and authors_raw: "Cpe N" — OCR noise off a scanned title page of the WHO Editorial Style Manual. 9789241548960-eng has three renderings of one title from the PDF (Handbook forGuideline Development 2nd edition from joined title lines, GRC Handbook - second edition from PDF docinfo, and the real one) and no authority among them. The IRIS record settles both. A library entry’s title is taken, in order, from: . | the catalogue record: dc.title of the Dublin Core record that the catalogue node naming the entry (libraryId) points at through metadataRef; | referenced.json identity.title; | the PDF Info /Title (structure.json metadata.docinfo.Title), only when it is not junk such as Microsoft Word - …, a file name, untitled, or an arXiv stamp; | the slug, which check:library-qa then reports as title-missing. | . The page-1 front-matter parse is never a title. It may still feed search and the section files’ doc_title. The manifest records which source won as meta.title_source (for example dc-record) and where it came from as meta.title_from, so R8 can be checked. The resolver is cat-harness-tools/pipeline/library-title.ts; the library-ingestion skill carries the full rule.

3635.title: Covers: an artefact we made, filed where IRIS files its own
3635.content: The replica’s home page shows a cover beside each item in its Recent Submissions strip, and each library entry page shows it too. None of them came from IRIS. Each is page 1 of the item’s PDF, rasterised by cat-harness-tools/scripts/pdf-cover.py and filed as a THUMBNAIL-bundle bitstream — the bundle name DSpace uses for the thumbnails it generates. Nothing downstream can tell the two apart from the bundle name, so the bitstream’s materialization.note must say the cover was derived here. The PDF is either held in this repository or, for a referenced item, fetched by the iris-cover-pdfs GitHub workflow, matched against the sha256 its ORIGINAL bitstream records, rendered and discarded. Only the cover PNG is committed. folio-assistant-core/scripts/gen-covers.ts (bun run iris:covers) renders only covers the catalogue asks for: a node declares the THUMBNAIL bitstream and the script supplies the bytes. It refuses to write bytes for a THUMBNAIL whose materialization.note does not declare the derivation, since a tool cannot attest to its own output. bun run iris:covers:check compares the bytes, the recorded sha256 and the recorded pixel dimensions, re-rendering where the PDF is held. That is R13 for covers. A cover whose PDF is not held can be verified but not re-rendered. The WHO emblem is masked on covers . The site chrome carries no WHO mark until the replica is published under WHO. Covers are shown with the WHO emblem and wordmark blanked to flat grey before the PNG is written, so the committed bytes never contain it. Each THUMBNAIL bitstream declares the blanked rectangles and the reason as maskedRegions. A title that contains “WHO” is not masked: it is the work’s name. A cover whose publication gates block it is shown as cover withheld, not no cover.

3636.title: Getting a record
3636.content: DSpace 7 exposes /server/api/discover/search/objects, paged and filterable by dsoType, scope and facets; communities are listed at /community-list. The calls this repository makes, and what live IRIS accepts, are in iris-rest-feed; the code is scripts/iris-cdn/rest-feed.ts. A record derived from a PDF rather than transcribed from IRIS must be marked derived, so it can be replaced wholesale when the real record arrives with nothing downstream having believed it. Enumeration cost, subsetting and the characterisation that decides whether IRIS may be cited at all are in who-iris/sources/who-iris.json.

3638.title: Oxigraph multi-graph search for WHO IRIS
3638.content: Skill iris-oxigraph: How to build WHO IRIS catalogue and Qualified Dublin Core metadata into partitioned N-Quads, and query it with Oxigraph — in Bun on the build side, in WebAssembly in the browser — including cross-graph joins and facet counts. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Adjudicate two KG extractors, GuidelineKG nightly path: verify and adjudicate the result, GuidelineKG nightly path: prepare the work order, GuidelineKG nightly path . The IRIS catalogue and its Dublin Core records are compiled into named graphs and queried with Oxigraph: natively in Bun at build time, and as WebAssembly in a browser. One SPARQL query can then join Dublin Core properties, catalogue containment and bitstream access gates — which DSpace Discovery cannot do in a single call.

3639.title: Build and query
3639.content: # Build from catalogue/nodes and site/dublin-core into dist/oxigraph/ bun run scripts/build-iris-oxigraph.ts # Build from exported DSpace records (the CDN release's records/ tree) bun run scripts/build-iris-oxigraph.ts --records <dir> --out <dir> # Load dist/oxigraph/who-iris-dataset.nq and run sample searches and facets bun run scripts/iris-oxigraph-search.ts bun test scripts/tests/iris-oxigraph.test.ts . scripts/iris-oxigraph-search.ts exports IrisOxigraphEngine (loadSpine, loadCommunity, searchSpine, complexSearch, facetCounts). The CDN exporter (scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts) calls the build over exported records and publishes each output file as graph/<file>.

3640.title: 1. Graphs and files
3640.content: The build writes, sorted and de-duplicated so unchanged inputs give byte-identical files: . | Tier 1, the spine — <https://iris.who.int/graph/spine>, in who-iris-spine.nq and .nq.gz. Hierarchy (dspace:Community, dspace:Collection), item Handles, titles, first creator, issued date, and bitstream descriptors with copyright verdicts. Loaded first. | Tier 2, one partition per community — <https://iris.who.int/graph/community/{id}>, in iris_who_int_graph_community_{id}.nq and .nq.gz. The full Dublin Core of that community’s items: MeSH authorities, abstracts, spatial coverage, govdoc numbers, ISBNs. Mounted on demand. | Catalogue and metadata graphs — <https://iris.who.int/graph/catalogue> and <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata>, each in its own iris_who_int_graph_{catalogue,metadata}.nq(.gz), and merged in who-iris-dataset.nq and .nq.gz for server-side use and integrity checks. | The documents’ reference lists — the folio-reference/v1 nodes in references/ (written by references:extract, one per entry a document prints). In the spine, the citation edges: the document’s Handle cito:cites the reference (https://litlfred.github.io/folio/references/<key>, the IRI its bibliography page names), and cito:cites the IRIS item when the library holds the cited work (heldAt). In the metadata graph and the citing document’s community partition, the reference itself: fabio:Work, dcterms:title or dcterms:bibliographicCitation (as printed), dcterms:issued (xsd:gYear), bibo:doi, dcterms:identifier. A document’s Handle comes from the catalogue node whose libraryId is its library slug. A --records build reads none unless given referencesDir. The bibliography’s own word search is a separate static index (<route>/search/, core’s bibliography-search.ts). | subgraph-manifest.json — the spine and each community partition, with file names, quad counts and item counts. | queries.json — prepared SPARQL queries. | . Namespaces . | dspace: = https://iris.who.int/ns/dspace# — catalogue terms (Item, inCommunity, hasBitstream, fileName, …). | dspaceNs: = https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/dspace/ — Dublin Core value terms, including authority. | . No binary bytes in the graph . PDFs, cover images and archives are never stored as literals. A bitstream node carries only: . | dspace:fileName (e.g. "WPR-RDO-2020-003-eng.pdf") | dspace:mediaType (e.g. "application/pdf") | dspace:fileBytes (integer) | dspace:copyrightGate — the copyright gate’s verdict, e.g. "permitted" | . The bytes are fetched from the CDN.

3641.title: 2. Requirements
3641.content: | # | Requirement | Why, in one line | . | OX-1 | Mint stable URIs at the extractor (https://iris.who.int/entity/item/{handle}#{prop}_{idx}); the build fails if any blank node remains | no multi-document collisions, every node addressable, no normalizer pass | . | OX-2 | Store zero binary bytes in RDF | keeps WASM memory small; binaries are static files on the CDN | . | OX-3 | Join across named graphs with explicit GRAPH blocks | separates containment and rights from bibliographic description | . | OX-4 | Use Handle URIs as the item subject (https://hdl.handle.net/...) | identity resolves outside WHO’s servers | . | OX-5 | Treat bitstream rights as access gates | results can be filtered by whether the PDF may be downloaded | . | OX-6 | Partition by community | a client fetches only the slice it needs | . | OX-7 | Never scan whole-corpus text in SPARQL | full text belongs in a static inverted index | . | OX-8 | Preserve controlled-vocabulary authorities (dspaceNs:authority) | distinguishes MeSH headings from free keywords | . | OX-9 | Append-only streaming partition emission | bounded memory at 300,000 items. Not met yet: buildIrisDataset holds and sorts every quad in memory; StreamingPartitionWriter is defined but unused | .

3642.title: 3. SPARQL recipes
3642.content: Recipe 1: multi-condition search . Items in the Western Pacific community, issued in or after 2000, with a subject containing “guidelines”, and a PDF whose copyright verdict is permitted. PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> PREFIX dspace: <https://iris.who.int/ns/dspace#> PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> PREFIX xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> SELECT DISTINCT ?handle ?title ?creator ?issued ?pdfName WHERE { # 1. Join Dublin Core Metadata GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata> { ?handle dcterms:title ?title ; dcterms:creator ?crNode ; dcterms:subject ?sNode . ?crNode rdf:value ?creator . ?sNode rdf:value ?subject . OPTIONAL { ?handle dcterms:issued ?issued } } # 2. Join Catalogue Hierarchy & Access Gates GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/catalogue> { ?handle dspace:inCommunity ?comm ; dspace:hasBitstream ?bs . ?comm rdfs:label ?commLabel . ?bs dspace:mediaType "application/pdf" ; dspace:fileName ?pdfName ; dspace:copyrightGate "permitted" . } # 3. Multi-Field Filter Evaluation BIND(IF(BOUND(?issued), xsd:integer(SUBSTR(STR(?issued), 1, 4)), 0) AS ?year) FILTER ( CONTAINS(LCASE(?subject), "guidelines") && CONTAINS(LCASE(?commLabel), "western pacific") && (?year >= 2000) ) } ORDER BY DESC(?year) . Recipe 2: facet counts . Item counts per subject term and its authority. PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> PREFIX dspaceNs: <https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/dspace/> SELECT ?subject (COUNT(DISTINCT ?handle) AS ?itemCount) ?authority WHERE { GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata> { ?handle dcterms:subject ?sNode . ?sNode rdf:value ?subject . OPTIONAL { ?sNode dspaceNs:authority ?authority } } } GROUP BY ?subject ?authority ORDER BY DESC(?itemCount) ?subject .

3643.title: 4. Browser pattern: spine first, communities on demand
3643.content: import oxigraph from 'oxigraph'; // Where the graph files are served from, e.g. a release's graph/ directory. const BASE = '<graph-base-url>'; async function gunzipText(resp: Response): Promise<string> { const stream = resp.body!.pipeThrough(new DecompressionStream('gzip')); return new Response(stream).text(); } const store = new oxigraph.Store(); // 1. Fetch the spine and the manifest const [spineResp, manifestResp] = await Promise.all([ fetch(`${BASE}/who-iris-spine.nq.gz`), fetch(`${BASE}/subgraph-manifest.json`), ]); const manifest = await manifestResp.json(); // 2. Load the spine: hierarchy, title search and rights filtering work now store.load(await gunzipText(spineResp), { format: 'application/n-quads' }); // 3. Mount a community when the user selects it. load() adds its named // graph without clobbering what is already in the store. async function mountCommunity(commId: string) { const partition = manifest.tiers.tier2_communities.partitions[commId]; if (!partition) return; const resp = await fetch(`${BASE}/${partition.fileGz}`); store.load(await gunzipText(resp), { format: 'application/n-quads' }); } // 4. Run a prepared query locally for (const binding of store.query(myPreparedQuery)) { console.log(binding.get('title').value); } .

3645.title: Reading IRIS changes over DSpace REST
3645.content: Skill iris-rest-feed: How to read changes from the WHO IRIS DSpace 7 REST API: the nightly “changed since” walk over Discovery, the weekly reconciliation that stands in for the deletions REST does not report, and the guard that stops a short listing from reading as a mass withdrawal. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation . Changes are read from the DSpace REST API only. REST has no change feed with deletions, so a nightly walk is paired with a weekly reconciliation. The code is scripts/iris-cdn/rest-feed.ts; its tests run on fixtures in scripts/tests/iris-cdn.test.ts.

3646.title: What live IRIS accepts
3646.content: . | Discovery offers only five sortOptions: score, dc.title, dc.date.issued, dc.date.accessioned, dc.date.available. sort=lastModified,DESC returns HTTP 422. | Changes are found with a Solr range query instead: query=lastModified:[<isoZ> TO *]. | The bound must be a Z-suffixed UTC timestamp. A +00:00 offset returns totalElements: 0. | .

3647.title: Endpoints
3647.content: | Use | Request | . | Changed items since cursor | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&query=lastModified:[{isoZ} TO *]&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Weekly full item listing | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Collection-scoped batch (initial load) | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&scope={collectionUuid}&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Communities / collections with parent | GET /server/api/core/{communities|collections}?page=N&size=100&embed=parentCommunity | . | One item with its files and collection | GET /server/api/core/items/{uuid}?embed=bundles/bitstreams&embed=owningCollection | . | Bundle bitstreams beyond page 0 | GET /server/api/core/bundles/{bundleUuid}/bitstreams?page=N&size=100 | . | A file’s bytes | GET /server/api/core/bitstreams/{uuid}/content | .

3648.title: Nightly: changedSince(cursor)
3648.content: . | Normalise cursor to UTC Z (new Date(Date.parse(cursor)).toISOString()) and run the range query above. | Page through the matching result set. | The cursor is inclusive: an item modified at that instant is read again, not missed. Re-reading an unchanged item writes the same bytes. | Return the items oldest first, de-duplicated by UUID. | . The cursor is the newest lastModified read, kept in state/cursor.json. A failed night does not advance it.

3649.title: Metadata changes without the PDF changing
3649.content: A PDF may stay the same while its Dublin Core changes. Records and files are handled separately: . | A record is re-read whenever its item appears in the walk. A PDF is re-fetched only if its DSpace MD5 changed. | Communities and collections are re-read in full every night (allContainers). A renamed collection changes no item, and DSpace 7 does not expose lastModified for these. An unchanged one serializes to the same bytes. | The weekly metadata check. The weekly listing pages carry each item’s metadata. metadataSha hashes it canonically, and any item whose hash differs from the one last ingested is re-read. That catches edits that did not move lastModified, without one fetch per item. | .

3650.title: Weekly: allItems and withdrawnOrHidden
3650.content: . | List every item ID Discovery returns. | Compare that list with the IDs the library holds. | Guard. If more than 1% of held items are missing, the listing is treated as faulty and nothing is marked. Possible causes are a paging fault, an outage or a Solr reindex. | Re-fetch each missing item by ID. Mark it withdrawn only if IRIS confirms it: withdrawn: true, or a 404 (gone), 401 or 403 (private). | .

3651.title: Fixity
3651.content: DSpace reports an MD5 checkSum for each bitstream. Downloaded bytes must match it before their SHA-256 is recorded. A mismatch quarantines the bitstream and reports it. It is never retried silently.

3652.title: Politeness
3652.content: Requests are made one at a time, with a User-Agent that names the project and its repository, and back off on 429 and 503. The initial load is paced to the budget stated in Task_StateBudget (processes/iris-cdn-initial-load.bpmn), including maxRequestsPerSecond.

3653.title: A subset by reference: run.ts subset
3653.content: bun scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts subset catalogues part of IRIS without fetching any bytes (who-iris#207): for each item, the Dublin Core record as DSpace returns it and a referenced catalogue node whose ORIGINAL bitstreams link to https://iris.who.int/bitstreams/{uuid}/download. The subsets it reads live in scripts/iris-cdn/subsets/. | Which items. A handles file goes first (for example the IRIS items a DAK cites), then a Discovery query. The query is a field query on metadata (dc.title, dc.subject, dc.subject.mesh, dc.description.abstract), not a bare keyword. A bare keyword also searches the PDF text, so vaccine matches a report that mentions one in passing. | Write boolean operators in capitals. Solr reads a lowercase or as a word: HIV or immunization or vaccine matches fewer items than vaccine alone. | A Handle to an item: GET /server/api/pid/find?id=hdl:{handle} answers 302 to /server/api/core/items/{uuid}. | An ISBN or govdoc to an item: query=dc.identifier.isbn:"{isbn13}" or query=dc.identifier.govdoc:"WHO/HIV/2017.09". | A sample is one-row pages at seeded random offsets, so the same seed gives the same items. | No fixity is claimed. IRIS reports an MD5. A sha256 is recorded only once the bytes are fetched (R13), so the MD5 goes in the bitstream’s note. | Hand-made nodes win. An item whose Handle or UUID another node already carries is skipped and reported. The tool rewrites only its own nodes, the ones whose note starts “Catalogued by reference by scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts subset”, and only when they changed. | A token, when IRIS gives one, comes from the IRIS_DSPACE_TOKEN environment variable as Authorization: Bearer …. It never appears in an argument, a file or a log. | .

3655.title: Knowledge Graph separation — the method
3655.content: Skill kg-separation: Separate a Knowledge Graph into its own repository — as a CONTENT repository (files to read, no code) and a TOOLS repository (the code that writes and checks it) — once it is too large, or its consumers or cadence differ. The end-to-end method: the signals that trigger it, the preconditions, eleven stages each with the command that gates it, the owner’s decision points, how identifiers, QA and publication move, how the parent consumes the result, rollback, and the post-move sweep that a move between the pair owes before the parent re-pins. graph-detanglement owns stages 1–3; this skill owns the rest. Bootstrap + bootstrap-tools and cat-harness + the tools layer are the worked examples. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release, Adjudicate two KG extractors, GuidelineKG nightly path: verify and adjudicate the result, GuidelineKG nightly path: prepare the work order, GuidelineKG nightly path . Skill id: kg-separation · Package: graph-management Process: kg-separation.bpmn . This is the replicable method for separating a Knowledge Graph that is too large to handle, or whose consumers differ, written from what the bootstrap separation did. graph-detanglement is the practice for stages 1–3 (declare in place, detangle, isolate). Read it for those; this skill points to it and does not restate it. Everything from “split the tools out” to “the parent’s copy is deleted” is here.

3656.title: When — the signals, and none of them alone
3656.content: Separate when the graph is too large to handle, or when a business reason separates it: “split only where consumers or cadences differ”. Size is often not the reason — bootstrap is 33 files and left because its readers and its release cadence differ from cat-harness’s. Record the signals in the work item before deciding: . | signal | how it is measured | . | files and bytes per layer | git ls-files \| cut -d/ -f1 \| sort \| uniq -c | . | clone cost | bun run cat health → repository-size | . | gate time a content change pays | bun run cat gates (the gate count and wall time) | . | merge contention | commits per day on main; PRs re-conflicted before merge | . | cohesion and cut of the candidate | bun run cat kg:detangle | . | wrong-direction edges within one layer — modules bucketed into the proposed repos by path rule | check:partition (its root is ONE layer; read the scope it prints) | . | wrong-direction edges between layers — checked against each one’s declared needs | bun run cat kg:detangle:direction, blocking in CI | . | wrong-direction references — the prose axis, not the import axis | check:reference-direction | . | what the tools would drag along | the import cone of the would-be tools package (check:tools-closure once it exists) | .

3657.title: An example pointing up is a mention, not a dependency
3657.content: check:reference-direction holds that nothing names a layer that depends on it. One kind of pointer does not break that rule: a lower layer citing a source as an example, where the one copy of that source lives in a layer above it. For example, a base IG layer’s document kind and voice quote a draft reference architecture whose library entry belongs to a folio above it; two copies of one key break the bibliography build, so: . | One copy. The source’s library entry lives only in the layer that owns it. The lower layer deletes its copy and never re-ingests it. | The lower layer keeps a pointer. A document-kind source’s ref is a URL to the owner’s published library page (DocumentKindSourceSchema allows “a library entry id or a URL”). A voice source names the owning repository in instance and adds its url. A quote keeps its libraryId and sectionId. | It is checked where the copy is. The lower layer cannot read the sections, so its quote check reports such a quote as “an example held by , not checked here". That is not a pass and not a failure (https://github.com/litlfred/smart-base/blob/main/scripts/gen-dth-term-findings.ts, `EXAMPLE_POINTERS`). | It is a mention. The lower layer’s build does not need the higher layer, and nothing it runs reads through the pointer. The URL form is already an address under check:reference-direction’s URL exemption (“a location is where a thing is, not a dependency on it”). A pointer that something would need to resolve in order to build is a dependency, and the content moves up instead. | .

3658.title: Preconditions
3658.content: . | Names agree before the cut — directory, declared name, package name. A rename after the cut is a cross-repository change. | One directory per layer, so extraction is one move, not a sift. | Every gate that guards the boundary has been watched failing — plant a violation, see it red, remove it. A boundary gate can pass while guarding nothing: unable to fail, blind to side-effect imports, or blind across layers. | The owner’s decisions are recorded in the work item (the list below). | “Generated output is the contract” is written down: what crosses the boundary is the generated file, and any tool may produce it. | .

3659.title: The pair: a content repository and a tools repository
3659.content: A separated Knowledge Graph is two repositories, not one. |   | content (<name>) | tools (<name>-tools) | . | holds | files to read — .md, .json, .bpmn, generated schemas, READMEs, diagrams | the code that writes and checks the content — Zod sources, generators, README/diagram writers, content checks | . | code | none (FR-7 — a reader needs nothing installed) | yes, with a declared, minimal dependency set | . | depends on | nothing | the content, and nothing above it — check:tools-closure | . | is used by | the parent harness, pinned | the content’s own checks, and the parent (a package) | . The rules of the pattern: . | The Zod source moves DOWN into the tools repository — not up into the harness. Zod in the harness makes a content release wait on the harness, which itself needs the content: a cycle. | The tools repository owns the content checks AND the README and diagram writers — one copy, which the parent harness also calls. It is not a second harness: a content Knowledge Graph declares no visualisers. It is one toolset over swappable content, so a different visualiser is a different toolset. | Every tool is a script an agent runs as the actor in a process step. Agentic first. A GitHub Actions workflow may be described, but ships disabled, and nothing that costs money runs unless the owner asks. | Harness output ABOUT the content stays with the harness (hosted): its QA verdicts (kgQaHomeFor), translation templates (translationsHomeFor), exported graph and glossary ledger. The content repository carries only what its own checks need. | . Staged content with no tools repository yet — the finding, not the silence . A layer can be planned as a content repository before its -tools pair is authorised. Declare it — separation: "content" in <name>.json; the content half of an existing pair is read from the tools layer’s supports and needs nothing — and kg:audit’s content-instance-holds-code records a finding naming every code file still inside it. It is a minor QA warning, not a failure, because the tolerated set is small; a warning still names each file, so the violation is never silent. The remedy splits by what the code is: generic code (it works for any instance of its kind — any DSpace catalogue, any PDF) moves into the platform and takes the layer root as an argument; layer-specific code waits for <name>-tools.

3660.title: The stages
3660.content: Each stage names its lane (a role in scenarios/roles.json) and the command that gates it. A stage is done when its gate is green, never when the work looks finished. | # | stage | lane | gate | . | 0 | Brief, measure the signals, claim | authoring-agent | signals in the work item; bun run cat beans:claim <id> | . | 1–3 | Declare in place, detangle, isolate | authoring-agent | graph-detanglement — all its gates | . | 4 | Identity: name, version, iriBase, needs, nodeSchemas in the declaration; move the base once | platform-authoring-agent | iri:sync -- --from <old base> then iri:sync:check; check:node-iris | . | 5 | Hosted outputs out of the content | platform-authoring-agent | the content leak test’s pending list is empty | . | 6 | Split content from tools: create <name>-tools/ as a sibling, move the code, cut its import cone | platform-authoring-agent | FR-7 (content holds no code); check:tools-closure; generated files byte-identical before and after | . | 7 | Publication plan: every identifier the content mints is a file some step publishes, at /v<major>/ | publication-manager | check:node-iris; the site layout in instance-publication §”The release site” | . | 8 | Rehearse standalone: copy content + tools alone into a temporary directory and run the tools’ checks there | build-pipeline | green with nothing else on the path; an empty tree exits non-zero | . | 9 | Authorise — report what moves, sizes, what breaks, and wait | administrator | the owner’s answer (deletion-requires-confirmation) | . | 10 | Seed: the owner creates the repositories; once the source has settled, seed main, then the content and tools as reviewed PRs, with history | administrator, then authoring-agent | bun run cat seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse answers settled for each layer, at seed time; then the seeding PRs reviewed and green | . | 11 | Parent consumes, additively: pin (a SHA while staging, a version once released), repoint imports, keep the parent’s copy. After any move of files between the pair, run the post-move sweep first (below) | platform-authoring-agent | the parent green with the dependency declared; check:published-refs; every gate in the sweep table | . | 12 | First release: tag, publish /v<major>/ | publication-manager | check:version-bump; every identifier dereferences (publish-verification (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) | . | 13 | Cutover: the one commit retiring the parent’s copy into fsh-guts as a verified archive (the deposit state:seed --cutover makes: it must extract to the exact tree removed, with a provenance note), deposited into the PARENT’s fsh-guts before the removal, frozen, never refreshed or rendered: a relocation, not a deletion (sub-kg-lifecycle stage 13 has the steps) | administrator | only after 11 and 12 are green; DONE only when bun run cat separation:cutover:check --site, run in the separated repository, exits 0 (Tool separation-cutover-check: mounts, declarations resolve, no monorepo wiring, layer direction, the site builds from the mounts alone) | . | 14 | Independent refinement: each new release adopted by the parent as a reviewed step | authoring-agent | upstream-version-adoption | . Nothing is committed to the new repositories before stage 10, and stage 10 starts only when the owner says so. Until then the pair is staged as sibling directories in the parent (bootstrap/, bootstrap-tools/). Ready to seed? — asked at seed time, not at rehearsal . A seed is a snapshot: one commit that names the source sha, with no history. Every open PR whose diff touches the layer when the snapshot is taken is orphaned into the monorepo: after cutover its change is in neither the seed nor anywhere that reads it. Stage 8 asked whether the layer stands alone, but the tree has moved since. So GW_SeedReady sits between creating the repositories and seeding them, and asks again: . bun run cat seed:ready --layer cat-harness --rehearse --text # exit 0 settled, 1 not yet, 2 unknown . | criterion | not yet when | . | heavy movers | an open PR labelled heavy-mover touches the layer or the next one up | . | next layer | any open PR touches the next layer up, which imports this one | . | layer load | more than five open PRs touch the layer | . | moves | an open PR deletes a file in the layer, or renames one into or out of it. A generator’s own names do not count: an owned-tree path in merge-conflict-patterns.ts (content-hashed payloads, rail data) is renamed by every regen, so moving one changes what no seeded path means | . | standalone | bun test is red with only the layer and what it needs beside it, as sibling directories | . | upward paths | a path DECLARED in the layer — a Tool module, a QA criterion source, a render target — resolves only in a layer above it, so it breaks the day the layer stands alone | . A test about the WHOLE CHECKOUT lives at the top. A test that reads several sibling layers at once, or the aggregate root itself (.github/, .gitignore, the root declaration, beans/, todos/, memory/, fsh-guts/), is red in every layer it is placed in, so it goes in the root layer’s DECLARED test home — folio-assistant-tests in folio-assistant.json, at test/ — never in a layer and never at a path a runner hardcodes. Whatever names every layer belongs at the top, so each layer below stays standalone-green. Split a file when only some of its tests read the checkout, keep the fixture tests with their layer, compose the moved paths from ORIGIN_DIR (the directory the test was written in), and move a corpus describe whole when it carries a vacuity guard: a sibling left behind passes standalone over nothing. A test reading an UPPER layer’s files moves to that layer. It is red standing alone for the same reason, one level down: the file it reads is not in its layer’s closure. It goes in the upper layer’s DECLARED test home, which may import the lower layer — never the reverse — and it is split, pointed back to and composed from ORIGIN_DIR exactly as above. Check first that the file it reads really IS the upper layer’s: a path written from the checkout root (cat-harness/src/… read relative to the working directory) is red standing alone over a file the layer does hold, and the fix there is to resolve it from the test file, not to move it. A test that reads the checkout’s GIT asks which of two things it is. A standalone layer is a fresh clone with no origin and one commit, so a test handed this checkout’s remote, HEAD or origin/main fails there on a missing input. A test of LOGIC that merely reads git — address derivation, an upload URL’s shape, a commit IRI, resolving a short sha — builds a throwaway repository whose facts it sets (gitFixtureRepo in cat-harness’s test/support/git-fixture.ts) and passes that root, with every assertion exactly as strict; a function that resolves its root internally gains an optional root parameter defaulting to today’s. A check that THIS repository is configured right — its own Pages address, its committed pages’ banners — keeps its assertion verbatim and moves to the top-level test home above. upward paths counts what breaks, not what is out of sight. It counts declared paths that resolve above the layer, not dependents discovery cannot find: discovery is checkout-local on purpose, so a count of what it cannot see never reaches zero, and the risk is paths, not layers. A seeding pair is not upward. A higher layer’s Tool nodes may resolve into their implementer below through needs; the two are seeded in the same step, so none of those paths can break on seeding day. The HIGHER layer says so, seedsWith: [<lower>] in its declaration, because a lower layer naming one above it is the wrong direction. seed:ready states such paths in its note and does not count them; a path into any other layer above still counts. Four things to keep straight: . | The layer map is read off the declarations: livesAt.path is the directory, the longest needs chain is the depth, and the next layer is every layer one level up that needs this one. Nothing in the tool names a directory. | Every threshold is in the decision table, processes/kg/decisions/seed-readiness-gate.dmn. The script works out each criterion’s verdict by evaluating the table with the other facts at zero, so changing “five” is a one-line edit to the table. | heavy-mover is a label a person applies. With none on the layer, the criterion passes. If the label cannot be read, the answer is could-not-determine. | The rehearsal runs only on request, with --rehearse. It copies the layer and its needs into a scratch workspace (~150 MB and ~8,000 tests for cat-harness) and refuses to start with less than 3 GB free. Without --rehearse, the standalone criterion is could-not-determine, so seed:ready cannot answer settled until a rehearsal has run. That consequence is the one constant SETTLED_REQUIRES_REHEARSAL. | . Could-not-determine is never clean. GitHub lists at most 3,000 files per PR, so a criterion that the unseen files could change is undetermined, and the gateway answers unknown and stops. An unknown only withholds settled, though. It never hides a finding that is already certain, so the table tests the not yet rows first. not yet goes to Drain: land, close or re-target the PRs it named, then ask again. The tool only reports. It never seeds, labels or comments.

3661.content: An agent asks these; it does not settle them. | Separate at all, and where the boundary is — after the signals are measured. | The address base for the extracted graph’s identifiers: under the parent, or the new repository’s own. | Where verdicts about it live: hosted in the harness, or in the content. | What the tools repository owns, and how its checks run (agent, package, described workflow). | Authorise the extraction (stage 9). | Whether the first release is a draft with a tag, or the first formal publication (instance-publication). | The cutover (stage 13). | .

3662.title: Identifiers and versions
3662.content: One iriBase and one version in the declaration. Identifiers a program reads and pages a person reads are both <iriBase>v<major>/…; the exact release is the pin’s (bootstrap-tools/schemas/release-iri.ts). A base move is bun run iri:sync -- --from <old base>, once. A $schema tag carries its schema’s own semver. The exported graph’s own @id moves only when the new repository actually publishes. A published node’s identifier must be its file’s path (check:node-iris).

3663.title: Versions of the pair — same scheme, same start, then independent
3663.content: . | At the split, both start at the content’s current version, for simplicity — bootstrap was 0.1.0, so bootstrap-tools starts at 0.1.0. | After that each is versioned on its own, by the same rules: semver, the bump computed from the exported surface (check:version-bump). | Tags are plain v<major>.<minor>.<patch> in each new repository: a standalone repository holds one layer, declared at its root, so the tag needs no name. check:version-bump reads the plain form only there; a repository of several layers — the parent while the pair is staged — keeps <name>-v<major>.<minor>.<patch>, because a plain tag could not say which layer it released. | A tools release says which content versions it handles as a list of supported MAJOR versions (bootstrap: [0]), never a range expression — instance-versioning rule 2 forbids range syntax, and within one major a newer minor or patch only adds (tagCompatible). A tool asked to work on a content major it does not list refuses rather than guesses. | .

3664.title: How the parent consumes the pair
3664.content: No git submodules, ever (remote-mount.md). | mechanism | when | details | . | Remote mount (remoteMounts) | staging & development | A declared directory fetched at a pinned 40-character SHA with a committed lock (index.lock.json) and consent record. Downstream checkout .gitignore automatically ignores mounted directory trees. | . | NPM KG retrieval (kg-retrieve-npm) | packaged distribution | package.json declared in <instance>.json (role: "package-manifest"). Tarball packed via pack-tarball with a folio-binary-release/v1 integrity record, downloadable via npm install or GitHub binary releases (unhydrated source vs hydrated store). | . | Package import | published tools | The parent imports the tools’ Zod schemas and pipeline writers as an npm package dependency. | . | Upstream pins | maintenance | upstream-pins.json, maintained by upstream-version-adoption.bpmn. | . Separation lessons . | Downstream Gitignore Contract: When remote mounts populate a layer directory in the consumer repository, the consumer’s .gitignore must ignore the mounted paths. Otherwise, git treats external files as uncommitted local files. index.config.json automatically includes all remoteMounts paths in the generated .gitignore. | Folded Layer Aliases: When a layer or subgraph is folded into another (e.g. cat-openapi folded into cat-harness as named subgraph openapi), external forks or dependencies may still carry needs: ["cat-openapi"]. schemas/kg/harness-config.ts maintains FOLDED_INSTANCE_ALIASES to resolve these. | Asset Permission & License Validation: Pre-separation audits must verify library/withheld.json and copyright gates. Materializing or mounting a separated catalogue without verified asset clearance causes 404s and broken links on published documentation. | NPM Manifest in the KG: package.json is an authored pre-packaging asset in the Knowledge Graph (role: "package-manifest"), and .tgz release tarballs are tracked as folio-binary-release/v1 state documents with SHA-256 integrity digests. | No Relative Directory Climbing Across Repositories: Once separated into standalone checkouts, climbing ../.. escapes the repository boundary into .claude/worktrees/ or the parent filesystem and fails with Cannot find module. All cross-repository imports MUST be authored as package imports (e.g. @litlfred/cat-harness/... or via package exports), or resolved through package specifiers / tsconfig paths, NEVER through escaping filesystem ../.. traversals. | No Fixed-Depth Repository Root Assumptions (REPO): const REPO = resolve(import.meta.dir, "..", "..") points at the checkout root in a monorepo and above it in a standalone repository, so the script cannot find <instance>.json or scans sibling worktrees. Resolve the root dynamically — search upward for <instance>.json, index.config.json, or .git. | Clean Standalone Manifest (package.json) and Tooling Scaffolding: When extracting a layer to an upstream repository, package.json must be normalized: . | Operational commands must live under "scripts", not leftover monorepo "checkoutScripts". | Script definitions must NOT hardcode monorepo subdirectory paths (e.g. "bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/..." -> "bun run scripts/..."). | A standalone tsconfig.json must be present to prevent tsc from walking up to the monorepo root. | Explicit dependencies and devDependencies must be declared. | . | Fan-Out Recursion Guard in declaringInstances: When a mounted dependency carries its own nested remoteMounts, consumer remote fan-out must not mount sub-layers into roots that are already locked mounts of the parent checkout (!lockedMountPaths(checkout).has(rel)). Otherwise remoteFanOut mutates the child checkout’s tree and treeDigest verification fails. | Relative Directory Symlink Handling in Staging & Tarball Scripts: Recursive copies (cpSync(..., { recursive: true })) of trees with internal symlinked directories can recurse forever. Staging, site compilation, and packaging scripts must copy symlinks with { dereference: false } or use archive utilities (such as tar or rsync -a) that preserve symlink references. | Purely Declarative Ontologies vs. Companion Toolsets (FR-7): Purely declarative base repositories (such as litlfred/bootstrap) contain zero runtime execution code, zero test suites, and zero package.json manifests (FR-7). All graph compilation (JSON-LD export, BPMN diagram rendering, site staging, and schema validation) is executed by the companion tooling repository (bootstrap-tools). The declarative repository marks its render exemption (renderExemption: true) in its root manifest, and tooling scripts accept an explicit target repository argument (--repo <dir>). | Toolchain Decentralization (package.json, tsconfig.json, bunfig.toml): Tools and harness subgraphs must possess full standalone toolchain autonomy. package.json must be a standalone package manifest (e.g. @litlfred/<tools-layer>), bunfig.toml defines test preloads per layer, and tsconfig.json must set "noEmit": true and omit rootDir/outDir to prevent error TS6059: File is not under rootDir when cross-subgraph schemas or utilities are imported. See bun-use. | Monorepo Coordinator Demotion: Once tools and code are extracted to their respective packages, the root package.json is demoted to a private coordinator ("private": true) with narrowed tsconfig.json (test/**/*.ts). The root platform coordinates development workspaces, mounts, and integration tests, but never directly exports or publishes tool implementations. | Ephemeral File Purging and Root Hygiene: Ephemeral generated directories (_kg/, build/, test-results/) must NEVER be committed to the root repository or left unignored. Build outputs belong to the tool that produces them. | Layer Memory Preservation: Root directories beans/, todos/, and fsh-guts/ are the layer’s own durable working memory (the agent’s plan, the user’s todo queue, and the archival store). They are never overlaid across layers, never extracted to downstream packages, and stay at root by design. | A cutover is not done until the layer has re-pointed and can publish itself: livesAt is not a comment — remote-mount.ts takes livesAt.path as the mount path and seed-ready reads it as “still staged”. A path that was only ever a mount inside the parent’s site build serves nothing on its own, and generated pages keep absolute links to the parent’s paths, which 404 once the bytes move. Before stage 13: livesAt is gone, iriBase is declared, and the layer’s own site builds from its own repository. | The replayer must never live inside a layer it replays: if every workflow (and every downstream folio’s staging build, through a reusable workflow) bootstraps by running a script inside the directory being retired, the cutover breaks the first step of every job. Before stage 13, grep every workflow the parent ships for paths into the directory being retired, and give the parent a bootstrap entry point that lives in the parent and needs nothing mounted (a dependency-free .github/mount-from-lock.sh that fetches the pinned replayer). | A downstream’s CI is part of “green” for a cutover: a reusable workflow called @main (uses: litlfred/folio-assistant/.github/workflows/folio-staging.yml@main) runs the PARENT’s current workflow in the DOWNSTREAM’s repository. A cutover that is green in the parent can therefore be red in every folio at once, and the red lands on whatever pull request the folio author opens next — it reads as their failure. Stage 12’s “green” includes one dispatched staging run of at least one downstream folio after the cutover commit. | A separated checkout must run its own tests and type-check its own subgraphs: run them in a fresh standalone clone. A test that reads <checkout>/../package.json fails with ENOENT outside the composed tree (lesson 6 by another route), and a tsconfig.json whose include omits named subgraphs (openapi/, archimate/) is green while never reading them. A test or type-check that silently depends on the composition, or silently skips part of the repository, is not evidence the separated repository works. | The kinds a declaration is judged against come from the checkout being read, not from where the harness module sits: the graph-typology registry reads the checkout under inspection first (defaultTypologyRoots; $REPO_ROOT still overrides), then its own; a kind both declare is shadowed and reported, never merged. Otherwise two layouts give two answers about one correct declaration. Every path a declaration names is resolved in one run by check:declaration-resolution, and separation:cutover:check uses it as its declarations condition. | .

3665.title: After a move lands — the post-move sweep
3665.content: Moving files between the pair is one reviewed commit in each repository; making the repositories that consume the move work again is most of the work. Run the sweep after a move lands and before the parent re-pins (stage 11), and do not call the move done until every gate in this table is green in a composed checkout at the matched pins. When another layer links into the moved path, declare the move first, so the layers can re-pin in any order: two-phase-move. | what still names the old home | the gate that catches it | the fix | . | A Tool node’s invoke.shell | kg:audit criterion tool-invoke-path-resolves (CRITICAL) | rewrite the invokes in each tools/<id>/<id>.json | . | Prose and commands in skills, guides, READMEs, BPMN documentation, workflows | check:command-paths | the rewrite rule below | . | A script’s own usage string | check:usage-paths | rewrite it in the receiving layer | . | Printed and RUN commands: “Run: …” remedies, generated banners, shell hooks, an e2e global setup | check:published-instance-exports, check:invocation-parity, security:gate (all three match paths by text), and the unit tests | rewrite the strings in the receiving layer | . | A wrapper generator’s list of the scripts it wraps | bat:sync / bat:sync:check (the writer errors on the first missing file) | update the list | . | Partition rules naming moved files | check:partition (“exact rule(s) name a file that is not in …”) | remove the dead rules | . | A kind-validator node pointing at a moved module | check:kind-validators:require-all | open: how a node in one layer names a module in the other | . | A writer’s claims in qa-refresh: files the writer used to rewrite became output it writes | qa:refresh (“N file(s) no declared writer claims”) | update the writer’s claims | . | A visualiser route a generator computed by hand | uml:overview inside skill:register (“no glossary page at …”) | use the declared route (declaredRoute(<core>, "glossary-page")) | . | A browser bundle importing a node-only module through a package import | navbar:assets (“Browser polyfill for module node:url …”) | move the constant into a node-free module | . | A directory declared inside another declared directory in the receiving layer | check:layout-norms (it stops qa:refresh) | move it out of the enclosing declared directory | . | A file left in BOTH layers | slice:sqlite / slice:sqlite:check (the KG export mints the same IRI twice and the slice dies on a UNIQUE constraint); node-kinds:check and kg:export do not refuse a duplicate on their own | delete the copy in the layer that no longer owns it, archived to fsh-guts/retired/ | . | Paired artefacts a move split across repositories | skills:docs (“page(s) produced by NO source”), check:declared-dirs (“absent — declared and not on disk”) | pin the receiving commits WITH the removing one (below) | . The rewrite rule . Rewrite a path only where the file exists in the destination and not in the source, and never in a record. The first half keeps a placeholder or a typo from turning into a different wrong path; the second keeps a file that moved and was later re-created from being redirected. Records say what was true when they were written, so they stay as written: proposals, todos, agent memory, work items, provenance (library figures, terminologies), upstream pins, vocab mappings, QA results and test fixtures. Generated files are rewritten by re-running their generators, never by hand. The rule is a Tool: rewrite-moved-paths (bun run cat paths:rewrite-moved --from-name <old> --from-root <dir> --to-name <new> --to-root <dir> --prefix <moved dir> … [--keep <glob>]). It reports with file and line by default, applies with --write, and with --check is the gate for a sweep that should be finished. Its test proves it never opens a proposal, a memory or a fixture. Pin the pair together, and record each consent first-hand . A move that removes files from one repository must be pinned together with the commit that adds them to the receiving one. A parent that pins the new source with the OLD pin of a receiving repository has the moved artefacts in neither, and the gates say so only indirectly. Before a re-pin, list what each new commit removes and confirm the receiving repository’s pin contains it. Every pin is a trust decision with its own consent (rule H8, remote-mount): trust.consent names who, when, the exact ref and the evidence, and mount:remote refuses a ref nobody consented to. A consent relayed by another agent is not the owner’s consent, so it is not recorded from the relay alone; record it when the owner’s answer to a question naming the exact SHAs is relayed verbatim with its time. A standing consent (“pin any main commit of these repositories that includes a fix merged in this session, listed in the PR”) covers only the repositories and the window it names, and each pin made under it is listed where the owner will read it. When a consented ref turns out not to do (a consented main with no declaration of the layer), do not substitute another ref: keep the previous pin and report it. The order that worked, and the rules for several sessions at once . | Fix the tools (the receiving layer): paths, the checks that matched paths by text, bundles, layout. | Fix the content (the source layer): prose, Tool invokes, declarations, partition rules. | Regenerate the content at matched pins, in a composed checkout laid down from the parent’s lock, to a fixed point (qa:refresh COMPLETE, then bun run cat regen, then every --check green on a fresh lay-down). | Re-pin the parent to those commits. | Run bun run cat gates on a fresh lay-down of the parent. | . When several sessions work on one separation at once: . | Hold pushes on a branch another session is superseding; hand over what is unpushed instead of racing it. | Announce which gates each session takes before starting, and re-check the open PRs and recent merges of a repository before opening one there. | Verify on the lock of the PR that will land, in a fresh scratch copy, never on another session’s checkout. | A measurement-only workaround stays local (for example a baseline entry needed to run qa:refresh while a decision is pending), is never committed, and is deleted once the real fix lands. | .

3666.title: Rollback
3666.content: Until the parent is green with the extraction declared, the extraction is additive and the parent keeps its copy; the cutover commit is the one unit worth reverting, and since the copy is ARCHIVED in the parent’s fsh-guts rather than deleted, the archive restores the exact tree that was removed. After a release, a tagged version is never reused: roll back with a new patch release and move the parent’s pin back.
