3675.title: Materializing remote content
3675.content: Skill materialize-remote: Landing remote content locally — the five gates, the three states, and the two purposes. One process, shared by catalogue import and harness bootstrap, plus the refresh that is not a re-import. Named by: GuidelineKG nightly path: prepare the work order . One process for every caller that lands remote content locally. | caller | remote source | held locally | refresh | . | the IRIS replica | IRIS | selected items | refresh-materialized | . | bootstrap | a harness | the cat-harness checkout | upstream-pins.json | . bootstrap/workflows/initialize-harness.bpmn fetches a harness that is remote content and lands it locally; upstream-pins.json exists because that copy goes stale. 3676.title: Ask the purpose FIRST
3676.content: working or archival, before any gate, because three of the five mean different things under each. |   | working | archival | . | what is kept | derived content — sections, OCR | the original bytes | . | retention | expires; re-fetchable | no expiry, by design | . | sourceLoss | unanswered | discharged | . | fixity | not needed | required | . A process that gated first and asked afterwards would be judging a copy whose obligations it did not yet know.

3677.title: The five gates
3677.content: Each is a decision a person makes; none is answerable from a file. A gate that only warns is a gate nobody fails. | Size — what fraction, and what the whole would cost. Refuse when you cannot tell: “three items” with no denominator is not a size answer. | Restrictions — “no restrictions known in context” is a state, not a green light. unknown is never rendered as permitted. | Copyright — per bitstream, and separately for the derived work. LICENSE-CONTENT.md exists here and the ingestion pipeline does not read it. | Retention — what expires this copy. A copy with no expiry cannot be told from an abandoned one. | Source loss — what survives if the origin goes. Only an archival copy discharges this. Origins do disappear: a regional repository instance can be merged away, taking its handles with it. | .

3678.title: Three states, and no default
3678.content: referenced (it exists, we know where, we hold no bytes) · materialized · unknown. A node that has not declared one is invalid, not unknown — “the author did not say” and “the author said they could not tell” are different facts, and only the second is actionable. A refusal is the process working. The node stays referenced, the graph still knows it exists, and the refusing gate’s basis is recorded so the next agent does not re-litigate it.

3679.title: Refresh is not re-import
3679.content: Three answers, not one: what changed upstream, what changed locally, and what to do when both. A materialized copy edited in place is not a copy — overwriting it destroys work whose existence was never established; check:materialized-fixity detects it. An archival copy is never refreshed. Re-fetching it discards the state it exists to keep. It gets a fixity check instead — has our copy rotted — which is a different question with a different remedy: restore from backup, never re-download.

3682.title: Adopting a methodology, and choosing between them
3682.content: Skill methodology-adoption: How a named external methodology enters the knowledge graph, and how an agent picks which one applies. Read before following a judgement method, before adopting a new one, and before writing a house method instead of adopting one. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load . A methodology is somebody else’s work, adopted whole. It is not a house process with a citation bolted on. The graph carries them as a distinct kind so that adopting one, replacing one and removing one are all ordinary operations. Methodologies are parallel ways of achieving the same process, chosen by context; each is formalised on its own and kept independent, so that other skills can incorporate it as a sub-graph.

3683.title: Parallel, not composable
3683.content: Two or more methodologies may answer the same question. Do not blend them. A composite — this one’s vocabulary, that one’s record, a third one’s filter — is a house method that cites nobody, and it inherits none of their authority while claiming all of it. So: pick one per decision, name it, and follow it.

3684.title: Choosing which applies
3684.content: First: is this a judgement, or a process? . Ask before the ladder. The ladder below is about how to decide something; a request for a change is not yet a decision but work needing agreed requirements before anything is built. Sent down the ladder, it lands on the catch-all rung and produces an options analysis for a question nobody has framed yet. Is somebody asking for a change, such that requirements have to be agreed before it is built? . If yes, the question is who is asking, and does the answer depend on what a folio says? . | A change to the platform’s own capability — a tool, a schema, a pipeline, a skill, a gate — raised by somebody building the tooling, whose answer does not depend on any folio’s subject matter → the software-development process methodology. | Requirements that come from stakeholders who must sign them off, tied to a folio’s domain → the stakeholder requirements methodology. | . Both answer request → agreed requirements, so they are parallel and must not be blended — the refusal below applies to this pair first and hardest. Which is which is stated in each one’s applies-when, not here, for the reason in §”Why this skill does not name them”. If no — the change is agreed and the question is how to decide something within it — continue to the ladder. Then the ladder . Ask in this order. The first yes decides. | Do the criteria recur, with the same inputs having to produce the same answer? → the computable methodology. A one-off tabled as if it recurs asserts a repeatability it does not have. | Is the question the certainty of a body of evidence behind a recommendation? → the evidence-grading methodology. Note this is about evidence, not about a design choice that happens to be uncertain. | Is the context a work item recording a decision? → the decision-record methodology. It constrains the record, not the method, so it composes with (1) or (4) rather than competing. | Otherwise — a one-off choice among candidate options → the decision-analysis methodology. | . If none fits, that is a finding, not a licence. Say which question the decision is and that no adopted methodology covers it. Do not improvise one and do not stretch the nearest fit: either is how a house method gets in. Why this skill does not name them . Naming each methodology here would couple this skill to the set, and the set is meant to be extractable: a methodology can be lifted out, or replaced, without a prose edit here. So the declared set is the contents of the methodology graph, read from the layer’s declaration. Ask for it; do not remember it.

3685.title: Node, skill, or both?
3685.content: An adopted methodology can produce up to two artefacts: . | you are writing | it is a node in the methodology graph | it is a skill | . | what the method IS — its vocabulary, its constraints, what it refuses | ✅ | ❌ | . | how to PERFORM it here — the extension element, the gate, the procedure | ❌ | ✅ | . | a house process with no external origin | ❌ | ✅ — and do not dress it as an adoption | . Most adoptions produce both, and the split is the same every time: the node is the method, the skill is this platform’s application of it. The skill names the node and does not restate it, because two files carrying one definition is two copies free to drift. Three worked cases: . | raci — both. The four letters and the one-Accountable rule are the method (node); reading R from the BPMN lane, the cat-harness.processes:raci element and check:raci are this platform’s application (skill). | crdm — both (methodologies/crdm.md). PHII’s three concentration areas (Business Process Analysis, Business Process Redesign, Requirements Definition), the Business Process Matrix, swimlane Task Flow Diagrams, and PATH’s activity-linked requirement structure are the external method (node, backed by library/phii-2023-crdm, library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, and library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm); agentic facilitation, 7-dimension code impact analysis, work-item decomposition, and pull-request merge sign-off are this platform’s adaptation (crdm-requirements-workflow and crdm-requirements-template). | swot — both. | . A methodology in use with no node is invisible to the graph: check:methodology-evidence and every other reader of the methodology graph count nodes, not skills.

3686.title: Adopting a new one — the ingestion process
3686.content: . | Establish it is external and named. A methodology has an origin: authors, a publication, a standards body. If it has none, it is a house process — write it as a skill and do not dress it as an adoption. | Render it faithfully, and say where the rendering stops. The file carries what the method says, not a summary of what we liked. Where this platform adopts part of a method and refuses part, both halves are stated with the reason — a silent omission misrepresents the standard. | Declare its applicability. applies-when in the front matter, phrased so the selection question above can reach it, and saying what it is not for. | Place it by ownership, not by convenience. A domain-neutral method belongs to the harness; a domain method belongs to the repo that owns the domain. The separation plan decides, and the placement must make extraction literal — the directory lifts out, its declaration entry goes with it, and nothing else moves. | Declare the directory. A methodology outside a declared directory is invisible to every tool that reads the graph. | State its refusals. The part of a method a platform must not do is as load-bearing as the part it follows, and it is the part a later agent will breach first. | Ingest the source and cite it as evidence. origin names the work; evidence: library/<bib-slug> points at a copy a reader can open from this checkout. Use literature-search to find it and library-ingestion to bring it in. Where the source cannot be fetched, that is an outcome to report — a located-but-unreachable document, never a missing one — and the node keeps its origin with no evidence until somebody closes the gap. | .

3687.title: Extract the PROCESS, not the paper’s tools
3687.content: A source that presents a method through an implementation is presenting two things, and only one of them is the methodology. Render the method first, then decide which tools — existing or to be added — this platform should use to perform it. A node that adopted the source’s tool stack would be adopting an implementation and calling it a method, and it could never be falsified: the tools would work and the method would never be examined. hybrid-llm-deterministic is the worked case. Its source demonstrates the method in one tool with one model and one expression language; the node renders the rule/result inversion, the five safeguards and the bounded-truncation technique, and §”Where this rendering stops” names every tool it declined to adopt and why. The method survives replacing all of them, which is the test of whether you extracted a method at all. Ask it as: what would still be true if they had built it differently? What survives is the methodology. What does not is their engineering, and it belongs in the skill if anywhere — where this platform’s own tool choices already live. And say what the source does NOT establish. A demonstration is not an evaluation. Where a paper shows an approach working once, with no baseline and no measurement, the node records that no performance claim rests on it. Doing otherwise manufactures a finding the authors did not make — the same failure as §”Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured”, arriving through a citation instead.

3688.title: An origin nobody can open is not evidence
3688.content: A methodology’s justification is being somebody else’s named, external work, so its origin must resolve to a source a reader can open. bun run cat check:methodology-evidence is the axis that makes this visible, and test/results/methodology-evidence.qa-results.json is where it is recorded. It reports and does not gate on a missing source: whether a methodology whose source nobody can open may still be used is the owner’s call, and a gate failing on the whole corpus at once would be switched off. It does fail on front matter that does not validate, and on an evidence pointing at a bib-slug no library holds, because a citation that claims to resolve and does not is worse than none. The evidence is an input to SELECTION, not only to adoption. options-analysis.bpmn’s A_CheckEvidence reads it before the chosen methodology is applied. Adoption happens once; selection happens at every decision, and a source can stop being reachable in between. A contested origin is recorded as contested. methodologies/swot.md is the worked example: the usual attribution is repeated everywhere and its own source says no academic reference supports it, so the node declines to name an inventor: flattening that into a fact would carry the authority of a citation while resting on nothing.

3689.title: Refusals
3689.content: . | Never blend two methodologies into one procedure. Parallel means parallel. | Never adopt a methodology by naming it. A citation with no rendered method is an appeal to authority that no reader can check. | Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured. Where a method scores and sums, this platform adopts the structure and refuses the arithmetic: a total reads as a measurement, and the weights were invented. This is the same rule as never quoting a count from prose as though it were evidence. | Never let a rejected option go unrecorded. Whichever methodology was used, the alternatives and why they lost are part of the output — the same argument bean-coordination makes for scrapped over deleted. | Never write a method from recall and cite a paper nobody fetched. Read the source, or say you read it through another and mark each attribution second-hand. See literature-search §”Never fill the gap with recall”. | .

3691.title: Does the prose say what the code does?
3691.content: Skill narrative-asserts-code: Judge whether the prose side of a declared prose ↔ code pair still says what the code does, when the machine could not settle it. Reads the two mechanical signals first — staleness and resolvable claims — and settles what is left in one of three ways, sending a disagreement with a checker to adjudication. General: the Lean case is a specialisation with its own skill. Named by: Adjudicate two KG extractors . A reader acts on what the prose says. When prose and code disagree, the reader either avoids a working feature or rebuilds it. This skill is the judgement step. The machine has already done everything it can, and your job is the rest.

3692.title: The pairs this applies to — declared, never inferred
3692.content: | pair | prose | code | declared by | . | diagram ↔ workflow | a .bpmn diagram’s <documentation> | the .github/workflows/*.yml it draws | # bpmn: <diagram> in the workflow (+ # bpmn-node: <id> per job) | . | skill ↔ code | a skill .md | the same-stem .ts beside it | the file sitting there | . | proof ↔ Lean | a paper block’s .md | its lean.ref | the block manifest — see below, it has its own skill | . A pair nothing declares is out of scope. Do not go looking for prose that “seems to describe” some code: an inferred pair is a guess, and a finding on a guess is how a check gets switched off.

3693.title: Read the machine’s output first — it is already in the sidecar
3693.content: Two kg-qa criteria on the subject’s sidecar tell you what is open: . | prose-reviewed-since-code-changed. fail means the code changed and the prose did not. It says nothing about truth, only that nobody re-read the prose. | prose-claims-resolve. Each claim the prose makes about the code comes out holds, false or undetermined. bun run cat pairs:claims prints the whole list, including what it did not check. | . What you judge is exactly the stale pairs, the false claims and the undetermined claims. A claim that holds and a pair that is not stale need nothing from you.

3694.title: Three outcomes, and each leaves a record
3694.content: . | The prose holds. Say why, in one sentence, and attest the pair: bun run cat pairs:attest -- --sidecar <sidecar> --by agent|human --reason "…". A reason is required because an attestation nobody can review is not evidence. Name what you compared: “the TypeScript step describes the repository gates and bun run cat gates derives its list from this job” is a reason; “looks fine” is not. | The prose and the code really disagree. Raise a finding against the side that is wrong. Usually that is the prose, because the code is what runs, but not always: a skill can state the intended behaviour correctly while the code has regressed. Say which side, and why that side. | You disagree with a checker’s false. The machine says a claim is false and you read it as true, or the other way round. Do not overrule it quietly. That disagreement is exactly what adjudication exists for: call Process_CriterionAdjudication (the QA-criterion specialisation of adjudication, whose outcomes are: the finding stands, the criterion is scoped, or a dispensation is granted), and the checker’s entry is kept beneath the verdict, because a disagreement between a checker and a reviewer is information. | .

3695.title: Lean is the specialisation, not the model
3695.content: For a proof ↔ Lean pair, a proof assistant can settle the formal claim mechanically, which no other pair kind allows. That work belongs to proof-narrative-lean-equivalence (the science layer): stub-weakening, overreach, hypothesis mismatch and notation drift. This skill states the question for every pair kind, and that one answers it for Lean. Nothing Lean-specific goes here, so a pair kind added later inherits the general question without inheriting Lean’s machinery.

3698.title: W3C N-Quads Dataset Packaging & Subgraph Distribution
3698.content: Skill nquads-distribution: How to compile, partition by named subgraphs, and distribute W3C N-Quads datasets beside pre-compiled SPARQL 1.1 named queries for static edge and client-side querying. Enforces upstream skolemization for zero blank nodes, partition size budgets, and single-source-of-truth publishing via declared served directories. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, GuidelineKG nightly path: verify and adjudicate the result . This skill governs the compilation, subgraph partitioning, packaging, and distribution of RDF datasets formatted as W3C N-Quads (application/n-quads) paired with audited, pre-compiled SPARQL 1.1 named queries. It provides a single source of truth across CLI, MCP tools, and static client-side web applications, enabling sub-second multi-graph query evaluation without running dynamic database servers.

3699.title: 1. Architectural Principles
3699.content: 1.1 W3C N-Quads Standards Conformance . | Specification: Conforms strictly to W3C RDF 1.1 N-Quads (w3c-n-quads). | Format: Line-based statement serialization: subject predicate object graphLabel? . | Zero Engine Lock-in: Oxigraph is the execution engine; the data format is strictly vendor-neutral W3C RDF. Any conforming triplestore/quadstore (Jena, Comunica, GraphDB) can consume these files directly. | . 1.2 Upstream Skolemization (Zero Blank Nodes) . | Blank nodes (_:b0) clobber each other across distributed documents and cannot be referenced across partitions. | Rule: Every compound node (e.g. Dublin Core qualified statements, MeSH authorities, work item notes) must be deterministically skolemized at intake into a stable URI: https://<domain>/entity/<id>#<property>_<index>. | Invariant: The dataset contains zero blank nodes (_:). | . 1.3 2-Tier Subgraph Partitioning . To prevent browser V8 heap exhaustion on edge devices, datasets are never delivered as a single monolithic multi-gigabyte dump. They are partitioned into two tiers: . | Tier 1: Global Routing Spine (<dataset>/spine): . | Contains the top-level hierarchy, IDs, titles, primary categories, and access gate verdicts. | Target payload: < 50 KB gzipped. Loaded instantly on application bootstrap. | . | Tier 2: Subgraph Partitions (<dataset>/subgraph/<id>): . | Contains detailed entity graphs (e.g. full Dublin Core metadata per DSpace community, or historical task audit logs). | Loaded additively and on demand when an agent or user accesses that domain. | . | . 1.4 Partition Size Budget . | Budget Ceiling: No partition may exceed 50,000 quads or 5 MB gzipped (enforced by MAX_RECOMMENDED_PARTITION_BYTES in schemas/kg/nquads-distribution.ts). | Protects mobile Safari and Chromium from OOM crashes during WASM decompression. | . 1.5 Git Hygiene: No Binaries in Repo . | Compiled .nq and .nq.gz files are never committed to Git. | They are generated during CI build or local execution into an ephemeral output directory, and served to GitHub Pages via mount-instance-docs through "served": true. | .

3700.title: 2. Checkable Requirements
3700.content: | # | Requirement | Why, in one line | . | NQ-1 | Strict W3C N-Quads Compliance | Prevents proprietary dialect lock-in; interoperable with any RDF store | . | NQ-2 | Zero Blank Nodes via Deterministic Minting | Blank nodes collide across document boundaries; stable URIs join cleanly | . | NQ-3 | Zero Binary Bytes in Quads | Keeps the graph lightweight; PDFs/images live in static CDN storage | . | NQ-4 | Partition Budget Cap (< 5 MB gzipped / 50k quads) | Prevents V8 heap exhaustion on mobile and edge devices | . | NQ-5 | Topology Manifest (subgraph-manifest.json) | Informs clients of partition quad counts, item counts, and relative URLs | . | NQ-6 | Pre-compiled Named Queries (queries.json) | Replaces arbitrary runtime queries with audited, injection-proof SPARQL | . | NQ-7 | Served via Layer Declaration (served: true) | mount-instance-docs.ts publishes files to _site/ without manual copy steps | . | NQ-8 | Single Source of Truth | CLI, MCP tools, and web browsers consume the exact same .nq.gz files | .

3701.title: 3. Concrete Implementations
3701.content: Implementation A: Document Repository Library Catalogue . | Compiler: scripts/build-oxigraph.ts | Spine Graph: <https://example.org/graph/spine> $\to$ catalogue-spine.nq.gz (communities, collections, handles, titles, copyright gates). | Subgraph Partitions: <https://example.org/graph/community/{id}> $\to$ community_{id}.nq.gz (Qualified Dublin Core, descriptors, spatial coverage). | Queries: search_by_mesh, filter_by_community, licensed_bitstreams. | Declared Served Directory: dist/oxigraph/ with "served": true in layer configuration. | . Implementation B: Folio Assistant Beans Work Plan . | Compiler: cat-harness-tools/scripts/beans-query.ts | Spine Graph: <https://folio-assistant.org/graph/beans> $\to$ beans-spine.nq.gz (every work item with its ID, status, parents, and dependency edges). | Subgraph Partitions: <https://folio-assistant.org/graph/beans/claims> $\to$ claims.nq.gz (session claims, burndown history, and audit records). | Queries: safe_drain_candidates, actionable_leaves, critical_path_blockers, rollup_invariant_violations, circular_blockers. | Declared Served Directory: beans/dist/ with "served": true in beans.json. | .

Run it before you push, not after CI tells you.

3725.title: The CI workflow is the list
3725.content: This skill does not list the gates, because a written list drifts from CI and a stale list reads as authoritative, so nobody checks it. bun run cat gates derives the set from .github/workflows/code-quality-gates.yml at the moment you run it, so a gate added to CI is in your next local sweep. package.json is not the authority: many of its check: scripts appear in no workflow, and running all of them would fail you on things CI does not gate. The workflow’s own comments name the scripts it deliberately excludes, with a reason beside each (for example check:ci-health is a report about main, not a gate on your diff). Read the reasons there.

3726.title: bun test green is not the gates green
3726.content: The test suite, tsc --noEmit and the *:check gates fail independently. One cause can also fail two gates at once. Run the gate set, not just the tests.

3727.title: …and the gates green is not the PUBLISHED PAGE green
3727.content: Gates read sources. A defect that exists only in a renderer’s output — for example markup that Kramdown escapes because a Liquid whitespace-strip joined two attributes — passes every gate. | Gate coverage is bounded by what a gate can look at. Ask what the gates read, not how many there are. | When your change alters a rendered page, build the page. The site build is not in the fast loop. check:escaped-markup asks one narrow version of “the output is well-formed”, and only in docs-site.yml, where _site/ exists. If the real build will not run locally (the just-the-docs remote theme 403s through the agent proxy), stub the theme and build anyway; never substitute the thing under test. continual-progress §”A template is not a page” carries the discipline. | .

3728.title: …and a green gate is not a VERIFIED FACT
3728.content: A gate can see the artefact and still answer a different question from yours. A rule that lives only in prose has a compliance ceiling nobody measures. When you write a rule into prose, ask what would fail if somebody ignored it; if the answer is nothing, you have written a wish. The measurable form is a check, a schema field, or a test. A gate’s silence is bounded by its stated scope. check:stale-paths, for example, judges two shapes — an id adjacent to an arrow, and a numbered step under a path heading — and declines everything else. Prose that merely mentions a closed work item passes it while carrying the same defect. Likewise check:ci-health labels workflow files that produced no run unjudged, not green. Green over a narrow rule is worse than red, because red is examined; a gate that does not fire is indistinguishable from one that passed. Before quoting a tick as evidence: . What does this gate say it judges, and is my claim inside it? . Read the check’s own header — every one here states its scope and its declined cases — rather than inferring the scope from the fact that it ran.

3729.title: Fast versus full is job membership
3729.content: The split is read from the workflow at run time. | fast — the typescript job. No browser. This is the inner loop. | --all — adds the jobs that install Chromium. render:bpmn:check is there because bpmn-js renders through a browser, so it can pass locally only because a browser happened to be installed. | . render:bpmn:check and node-views:report are QA reports, not merge gates: their results go to the qa-reports branch and show on each layer’s QA page, and neither is in index-gates.json or always-green. The node-view report needs a built site or a live base, so it is not in the fast set either; its author’s check is node-views:judge --against main, which fails only on a finding new against the baseline.

3730.title: Running “the gates that relate to my change” is not running the gates
3730.content: Pick the gate set by JOB MEMBERSHIP, never by which gates you judge relevant. bun run cat gates --all is the whole point of there being a command. A subset chosen by an author tests the author’s model of the change, and CI tests the change; they differ precisely where the bug is. gates --all takes minutes; a red CI run costs a push cycle. A verification names a tree . A verification names a TREE, not a branch. Anything edited after the run started is unverified, however green the run was. bun run cat gates reads the WORKING TREE, not the commit. An edit made while it runs leaves the change unverified, and can make the run report failures that were never in any commit. Nothing looks wrong when this happens: the run really passed, about a different tree from the one pushed. Run the gates after the last edit, not alongside it — if you edit while they run, the run is spent and needs doing again. A skill edit is the case most likely to produce this, because a skill body has two committed artefacts generated from it. A skill edit is three files: . | file | regenerate with | . | the body, skills/<pkg>/<name>.md | — you edit it | . | test/results/kg-qa/.../<name>.kg-qa.json | bun run cat kg:audit | . | docs/reference/skill-instructions/<name>.md | bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts | . The kg-qa row is a derived QA result whose record is the commit-keyed entry the CI job qa-publish stores on the orphan qa-reports branch. While a committed copy exists, kg:audit:check compares against it, so regenerate it. bun run cat skill:register does all of it in one command. A minted term needs a gloss . termIri("X") MINTS a term, and a minted term needs a gloss. Adding a new @type or a new property in kg-export.ts is therefore a TWO-file change: the emitter, and schemas/content/vocabulary.ts (CLASS_GLOSSES for a type, PROPERTY_GLOSSES for a property). ns:check refuses the half done alone. This is a different gate from the export’s own undeclared-term report: one checks that the JSON-LD @context binds the term, the other checks that the namespace DEFINES it. Both must pass, and passing the first is not evidence about the second.

3731.title: What a *:check failure is telling you
3731.content: Most of these gates compare a committed artefact against what its generator would produce now. A red one almost never means “the artefact is wrong”. It means you changed an input and did not regenerate. So the fix is to run the generator and commit its output — never to hand-edit the artefact into agreement, which makes the next regeneration noisy and detaches the artefact from its source. QA gates have a different shape. A gate over the qa graph computes and judges: --check writes nothing, and fails only on a finding that is NEW against a baseline — the committed working copy, or --against <ref> on the qa-reports branch. A missing baseline is UNKNOWN, printed and never a pass, never a fail. The four judge states are ok (0), finding (1), unknown and error (2) — JUDGEMENT_EXIT in scripts/qa-results.ts. A red one of THOSE is a real finding your change introduced; regenerating does not clear it, fixing the subject does. Which gates have this shape is in each script’s own docblock. Each *:check script has a generator beside it under the same stem; bun run cat gates:list shows the check, and the script it checks is named in the check’s own output when it fails.

3732.title: …and a green gate set is not a CLEAN RUN
3732.content: bun run cat gates snapshots the tree before the first gate and after every one, so every gate can pass and the run still exit 1: . ✗ every gate passed, and the run is NOT clean — 1 gate(s) changed the tree. The gates after the mutation were handed the repaired tree, so their verdicts describe a state you have not committed. gate-tree-mutation (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) carries the two causes, the one command that tells them apart, and the question that settles the second: does the churning field describe the subject the artefact is about, or the run that produced it? Only the first is a reason to write.

3733.title: Three things this skill will not do for you
3733.content: It does not replace reading the failure. The runner names the failing command and the CI step it belongs to, so a local failure and a red PR are findable by the same string. Read what the gate printed. It does not tell you a gate is wrong. A gate whose purpose you cannot state gets “fixed” by being made to pass, which turns the check into decoration. Every gate in that workflow carries a comment saying what it catches; if you think one is wrong, that comment is what you are arguing with. It does not make --all optional before a push that touches a diagram. Anything under processes/ changes a rendered SVG, and the check for that is in the browser job.

3734.title: If bun run cat gates reports no gates
3734.content: It fails rather than exiting clean: an empty sweep that exits 0 is indistinguishable from a passing one. If you see that refusal, the workflow was renamed or restructured and the reader needs fixing — not the gate list.

3735.title: Related
3735.content: |   |   | . | .github/workflows/code-quality-gates.yml | the authority, with a comment per gate saying what it catches | . | scripts/gates.ts | the reader, and the vacuity guard | . | continual-progress | commit early, open the PR at the first commit — this is the step before the push | . | prepare-merge (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | the pre-merge recipe, which runs these plus content-type gates | . | ci-health | whether the workflows themselves are working — a different question | . | gate-tree-mutation (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | reading NOT clean — a green gate set over a tree a gate repaired | .

3736.title: platform-gates (skill)
3736.content: The skill platform-gates as its source file cat-harness/skills/process/process-core/platform-gates.md writes it, rendered by gen-processes-viz.ts because it has no instruction page on this site — do not edit here. All processes .

3737.title: Prepare-merge — get a feature branch ready to land
3737.content: Skill prepare-merge: Take a feature branch to a clean, conflict-free, green, pushed state so it can be merged with no surprises: base merged in, generated files regenerated, the folio’s content-type gates run, then pushed. It does NOT merge and does NOT push to the default branch. Use for “prepare-merge”, “make it mergeable”, “ship it”. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release, Adjudicate two KG extractors, GuidelineKG nightly path: verify and adjudicate the result, GuidelineKG nightly path: prepare the work order, GuidelineKG nightly path . Canonical, repo-agnostic recipe for taking a claude/* (or any feature) branch to a clean, conflict-free, green, pushed state so it can be merged with no surprises. Downstream repositories vendor or sync it rather than maintaining their own copy. “Prepare-merge” is a plain-English ask, not a built-in command, so without one recipe each agent re-derives the steps, inconsistently or unsafely. “Prepare-merge” ≠ “merge”. It makes the branch mergeable and stops. It does not push to the default branch and does not merge a PR. Both are outward-facing, hard-to-reverse actions — do them only on an explicit request. The merge itself is its own sub-process with its own gate, merge-to-main: evidence on the head, the owner’s authorisation for THAT merge, recorded, then the merge. Asking for prepare-merge (or “ship it”) is not that authorisation.

3738.title: fsh-guts must not reach publication
3738.content: Before a branch that touches the knowledge graph ships, the published export must contain no reference to fsh-guts — not the graph typology, not the declared directory, not the skill that documents it, and not an edge naming any of them. scripts/tests/fsh-guts-unpublished.test.ts asserts it against the built artefact and runs in bun test. The mechanism is in kg-export §”fsh-guts NEVER reaches a published graph”.

3739.title: Recipe
3739.content: . | Clean + committed. git status --short must be empty. Commit outstanding work first (the container is ephemeral — uncommitted work is lost on resume). | Fetch the base + your branch (retry on network error, backoff 2/4/8/16s): git fetch origin <base> <branch>. | Integrate if the base moved. Compare git merge-base HEAD origin/<base> to git rev-parse origin/<base>: . | Equal → base hasn’t moved; nothing to do (your branch is a clean fast-forward). | Different → bring the base in, resolve conflicts, then re-run the green check. A rebase needs a force-push with lease: git push --force-with-lease — never a bare --force (it clobbers sibling pushes). | . Merge with bun run cat merge:main, never a plain git merge followed by regen. It resolves every conflict a declared pattern covers (glossaries, translated glossaries, UML, viewer pages, site data, QA sidecars), refuses the rest with the tree restored, and runs regen on the result. A plain git merge stops on those same generated files, one by one. After EVERY base merge, conflicted or not, run bun run cat regen — see §”A clean merge can produce a wrong artefact” below. If you merged with bun run cat merge:main, its regen already was that run; do not run a second one. For a merge whose conflicts were all generated, the round is merge-conflict-patterns §”A merge round — run each check ONCE”: targeted checks and a push, with CI’s sharded run as the full gate set in place of a local bun run cat gates or check:merged. An authored conflict, or a merge that touched code, still owes both. A conflict in test/results/ or test/attestations/: see §”Conflicts in test/results/ and test/attestations/” below before resolving either by hand. | Prove it merges cleanly (no assumptions): . | git merge-base --is-ancestor origin/<base> HEAD → success means a clean fast-forward, so conflicts are impossible. This alone is sufficient. | Otherwise dry-run with git merge-tree --write-tree origin/<base> HEAD (exit 0 = clean; non-zero = not clean; add --name-only to list the conflicted paths) and trust its exit code AND its first line. Exit 1 means CONFLICT only when stdout opens with the merged tree’s id — git also exits 1 for a ref it cannot merge (unfetched, mistyped), printing no tree, and that is “could not determine”, never “conflicted with nothing in conflict”. | Capture $? on the line after the command, before anything else runs — git merge-tree … >/dev/null 2>&1; rc=$?, or cmd || rc=$?. echo "base($(git rev-parse --short origin/main)) rc=$?" reports the SUBSTITUTION’s status, always 0 when the ref exists. if ! cmd; then rc=$? is the same trap: inside that branch $? is ! cmd’s status, 0. shell-exit-status.test.ts fails on either shape in a tracked script or workflow. | GitHub’s HTTP 405 “Pull Request has merge conflicts” is a backstop, not a check — it is learned at merge time, after the PR was announced clean. Do not grep the old three-arg output for <<<<<<< / “changed in both”: that false-positives on files which legitimately contain those literals (docs about merge conflicts, test fixtures, this skill). | A clean text merge is not a clean state. merge-tree answers “do the files conflict?”, not “do the gates pass on the result?”. Before asking for a merge, run bun run cat check:merged: it builds the merge with the current base in a throwaway worktree and runs the full bun run cat gates there (exit 0 passes, 1 fails, 2 could not determine — never read as clean). A generated measurement can be green on the branch, green on the base, merge without a conflict, and be stale on the result. | GitHub’s merge queue tests exactly the commit that will land; the gating workflows carry merge_group: so it works once the owner turns it on. Until then, check:merged is the agent’s half. | . | Green check. Run the project’s tests/build (here: bun test, plus bun build <file> --target=bun for type-checking touched files). Report honestly: distinguish failures you caused from pre-existing ones (diff the counts against a baseline run on the merge-base). Do not call a branch green by silently inheriting red. Then run bun run cat security:gate, by name, and quote its result. It runs every security check this repository has (workflow injection, secret leaks, lockfile and toolchain pins, QA reviewer permission, materialised fixity) plus two advisories, and refuses when a blocking check fails OR could not be run. Most of those checks are also inside bun run cat gates; naming the command here makes the merge step cover security explicitly, rather than only when the CI run before it happened to include it. Its advisories (unpinned third-party actions, dependency advisories) are reported in the PR and are not cleared by a green gate. Check the adversarial review verdict with bun run cat check:adversarial-review. On any branch with agent provenance (trailers, claude/* branch, bot committer), it verifies that an independent adversarial review verdict exists, binds to the head SHA, and covers the full diff without silent truncation. Findings are warn-only (“would have blocked”): they are recorded, as data for deciding when to promote the check to a gate, and do not hold the merge. Know what the target covered. Green is a claim about the files the build compiled, which is usually fewer than the files on disk — build targets default to a root plus its transitive imports. Confirm the files you touched were in it (artifact count vs. source count, or build the module by name), and scope any corpus-wide number you quote to what actually ran. For contentType: paper branches that touch content blocks, also run the block_pdf_render gate: . bun run scripts/render-changed-blocks.ts [--upload-drive] . This compiles a standalone PDF for every changed block and scrapes the LaTeX log; --upload-drive additionally pushes clean PDFs to Google Drive when it is configured. Exits 1 on LaTeX errors (fix required); exits 0 with warnings only (advisory); exits 2 on setup problems — including no local latexmk, which is the common case in a container. Exit 2 means the gate did not run; report it that way rather than folding it into a green. For a branch that changes a folio’s blocks, report review coverage. content-change-review.bpmn’s coverage gate (GW_Covered, table decisions/review-coverage-gate.dmn) reads the block counts below and, where the preview published a rendered-impact.json, three page counts (unreviewed pages, undetermined inputs, missed pages; see rendered-impact). Report them in the PR body, in the gate’s own terms, and a page count the preview did not publish as “not known”: . | open defects: review comments of kind defect still open or addressed, from the preview’s review-comments.json; | changed blocks with neither a verdict nor a waiver on their current version. | . Both come from one command, the folio-review-coverage Tool, run on the preview’s published files with --changeset changeset.json --blocks blocks.json --comments review-comments.json [--rendered rendered-impact.json --measured rendered-measured.json]. Its command line is the Tool node’s invoke, declared by the content layer that owns the review process. Quote its stderr summary. If the preview has no review-comments.json, or one with no verdicts field, write “not measured”, never 0. Never count resolved comments as coverage: a resolved comment is not a reviewer’s verdict on the block. This REPORTS; it does not merge or refuse. The gate belongs to the review process, and the committee decides the outcome. A branch like this is a content PR: label it content and write its ## Content review section before it is ready (§”Content PRs”). Say so when coverage could not be measured, because a branch passed with unmeasured coverage reads as “reviewed”. | Push the feature branch (retry/backoff as in step 2): git push -u origin <branch>. Then ask whether the push produced a run: bun run cat check:head-has-run. The push runs the fast gates first, where the pre-push hook is on. Git’s pre-push hook (installed by cat-harness-tools/scripts/git-hooks/install.sh) and, for agents, a Claude Code PreToolUse hook on git push both run cat-harness-tools/scripts/pre-push-gates.ts on the checked-out tree, before anything leaves the container (work items cat-tools-pp9g and folio-assistant-fn8q). It runs the fast gates minus the whole-suite bun test, plus only the test files whose import closure holds a file the push changed (owner, 2026-11-05: “Affected tests only”). CI still runs the whole suite. What it says: . | refused: a gate or an affected test that is green on the push’s base in this same environment is red now. Fix it, as you would a red CI job. It quotes the gates or tests and the log path; | ? gates not judged: a red it cannot attribute to this push (red on the base too, or no base outcomes recorded here), tracked files that differ from HEAD, exit 2, or no cat runner. The push goes and CI decides. A fresh container reddens some tests CI passes (no publish-time pages, a slower machine), so this is not a local green: report it as not determined, never as pass; | ✓: the fast gates passed on this tree and the affected tests with them. A record keyed by the tree is written; it names bun test as held out, so it never claims the suite. Pushing the same tree again re-runs nothing. | . A push the hook refused is never forced through with a bare --no-verify. If you must push anyway, name the reason, which is logged to .git/cat-gates/push.log: CAT_GATES_BYPASS='<reason>' git push ..., and put the same reason in the PR body. A local pass does not replace step 7: CI still runs every gate. This does not change what you do next — step 7 dispatches either way. It changes what you can honestly SAY. A push can silently produce no run, and a pull request showing zero checks is indistinguishable from one whose checks have not started (§Guardrails, “NO CHECKS IS NOT GREEN”). If the check reports no run, write that in the PR body alongside the dispatched run’s URL. Three states, and the third is not a finding: could not ask (no remote, no network, 403, 404) means nothing was established, and it must not be reported as either answer. | Dispatch the repo’s CI on the pushed branch, and fold the result into the PR. Local green is not CI green — CI runs on a cold cache, its own toolchain, and without whatever build flags you set locally. So after the push, trigger the relevant workflow against your branch (gh workflow run <wf>.yml --ref <branch>, or the actions_run_trigger MCP tool), wait for it, and put the run URL and conclusion in the PR body. Red → fix and re-dispatch. Do not open a PR citing a workflow nobody ran. If you lack actions: write and dispatch returns 403, do not quietly skip it: state in the PR that CI was not run, and give the exact command a maintainer should run. Find the workflow by reading .github/workflows/, not by name. Guessing a workflow name is how this gate gets skipped while appearing to run (a guessed name can be a publish workflow). In a repository whose workflows are all workflow_dispatch-only, nothing runs on push or PR, and “CI is green” is only ever true because someone dispatched it. Check when CI last ran (actions_list → list_workflow_runs): “there is a workflow” is not evidence anything is being checked. Many workflows document a local equivalent in their own header. Run those; they are the same check without the dispatch. Read the workflow before assuming there is no local path. | Stop here unless a PR / merge was explicitly requested. If a PR was requested, see below. | .

3740.title: What a green LOCAL run entitles you to claim
3740.content: The same commit can fail different tests in CI, in a clean worktree, and when the failing files are run alone, and the sets need not be nested. A green local run is not a weaker version of a green CI run — it is a different measurement, and either can be the one that is wrong. What it entitles you to say, exactly: . The gates I ran passed, on the tree I ran them on, in this environment. And what it does not entitle: . | “CI will pass.” CI tests refs/pull/N/merge, not your head — a tree neither parent holds. A staleness that exists only in the merge tree cannot be seen from any checkout. | “The gate set passed.” Only if you ran the gate set. A subset chosen by hand misses gates such as check:partition (a new script must be classified in scripts/partition/instance-rules.ts) and no check script is unrun (a new check:* needs a SCRIPT_EXEMPTIONS entry when no workflow runs it — or, for a script owned by a layer above cat-harness, a gateExemptions.scripts row in that layer’s <instance>.json). bun run cat gates derives its list from the workflow, so it cannot drift from what CI runs. | “Nothing is failing, so nothing is wrong.” A conflicted head produces no merge ref, so pull_request workflows never fire and the PR shows zero check runs. That reads as untested, not as red. | “It passed in isolation, so the failure is not mine.” Running the file alone removes the only condition under which it failed — for example a test near its time budget that crosses it only under load. | . Your environment is part of the claim, and it can be checked. Run bun run cat check:environment before trusting a run from any hand-built tree, and install dependencies rather than borrowing them: a symlinked root node_modules makes any tool that resolves a real path through it report a location this repository does not contain. Confirming the symlink is git-ignored is not enough; path resolution is a separate confound.

3741.title: A new gate in a lower layer must pass downstream (STRICT)
3741.content: A layer that adds a gate or a check:* script takes on its downstream layers too (owner ruling, 2026-11-07, card “Rule 13”: add it): the next re-pin of each one runs it. Twice on 2026-11-07 a lower layer’s main broke every downstream re-pin. New check scripts that no downstream workflow ran failed no check script is unrun (check:test-gherkin, and translation:page-qa:check, which also had a flag mismatch). Checks that walked the file tree without skipping declared build outputs failed too (two such checks in the tools layer). Each time, the re-pin became the P0. So, in the same PR that adds the gate: . | It passes on the layer’s own main. | It says how downstream layers run it: either wired through the shared reusable workflow, or declared opt-in per layer with an exemption row each downstream layer can carry. | A downstream dry run proves it: lay the branch over a fresh mount of folio-assistant main, and run the gate set there. Say in the PR what ran and its result. | . Without all three, the gate waits. It never lands for the next re-pin to discover. The converse holds too: a gate judges a repository against its own dependencies, never against a dependent’s pins of it. A gate that mounts a downstream index and so tests an older copy of the repository under review is a defect in the gate, and its red never holds the lower PR (merge-queue §”A lower repository never waits on a higher one”).

3742.title: A clean merge can produce a wrong artefact (STRICT)
3742.content: bun run cat regen after every base merge. Not only after a conflicted one — after every one. bun run cat merge:main runs it as part of the merge, so after merge:main it has already happened once and a second run re-asks the same tree. Two branches can change one committed generated file in non-overlapping places — say one adds a count field to a projection’s header and the other adds an entry to its array. Git merges them with no conflict and produces an artefact neither side would ever emit (a count that disagrees with the list). A conflict is a question. A clean merge is an assertion that the result is correct — and for a generated file that assertion is worth nothing, because git is merging text it has no way to evaluate. After a merge, RE-RUN THE GENERATORS. Never read the diff to decide whether you need to. bun run cat regen does it by asking each gate first, so its output is the set of artefacts the merge actually broke rather than a wholesale rewrite: . bun run cat regen # repair what is stale in the whole gate set bun run cat regen --fast # ...only the jobs that install no browser bun run cat regen --dry-run # report what is stale, change nothing bun run cat regen --changed <base> # ask only the pairs whose inputs changed since <base> bun run cat regen --explain # say, per pair, why it was asked or not . It asks the gates rather than regenerating everything because the gates (read from the workflow, not package.json) are the list, and because rewriting artefacts that were already correct leaves a diff that says nothing about what the merge broke. The QA working copy is part of the run — do not build it by hand around regen. Generators such as uml:overview and readme:subgraphs read the computed, ignored */test/results/ tree. Before every pass regen asks the copy’s stamp (bun run cat qa:working-copy -- --status) whether it was built from the tree as it stands, and rebuilds it if not. The paths that rebuild changed join the pass’s change set, so any pair that reads them is asked again. A failed build exits 2, and regen never grades a pass over a half-built copy. gates uses the same stamp, so the gates that follows a regen on the same tree builds nothing. It reports four states, and unrepaired is the one to read: a check that still fails after its writer ran is a real defect, not staleness, and the command exits non-zero rather than claiming a repair it did not make. So is a check with no writer. --changed asks less, and says what it assumed. A pair whose declared inputs, script sources and commands meet none of the paths changed since <base> (plus the working tree) is not asked: its answer is its answer at <base>. Undeclared and {tracked} pairs are always asked, as is any pair whose inputs cannot be determined. bun run cat merge:main passes the merge’s fork point, so a skipped pair is one NEITHER side touched, and it is current if the fork point, the branch tip or the base tip was current. merge:main -- --full-regen asks every pair. Separately, every pass after the first asks only the pairs whose inputs the previous pass actually changed (measured from git, not declared). Both cuts are only as good as the task-io.ts declarations — and, for a task owned by a layer above cat-harness, that layer’s own taskIo block in its <instance>.json. task-io.ts collects them and refuses a task declared twice, so declare a row where its script lives, never in both places. The whole-tree pairs (kg:audit:all:check, skill:register:check, kg:audit:check) still run after every merge. Submodules: check the pointers BEFORE you stage the merge (STRICT) . A base merge can roll a submodule back without a conflict, and git add -A is how. git merge updates a submodule’s gitlink in the index but not the submodule’s working checkout. If the checkout still sits at the branch’s old pointer, git add -A during conflict resolution stages that stale checkout, rolling the submodule back in the merge commit. bun run cat regen then runs against the old tools and “repairs” generated files to their old form, and CI fails in code the PR never touched. No step conflicts, and every local check against the stale submodule passes. So, after any base merge and before staging: . git submodule update --init --recursive # move each checkout to the merged pointer git diff --cached --submodule=short -- bootstrap bootstrap-tools # must be empty unless YOU bumped it . Then regenerate. Stage paths by name during a merge, never git add -A, and before pushing confirm the merge carries only your change: . git diff --stat origin/<base> HEAD # should list your files, not hundreds . A diff against the base far larger than your PR is the signal.

3743.title: Conflicts in test/results/ and test/attestations/ — regenerate one, read the other
3743.content: | tree | holds | durable home | on a conflict | . | <instance>/test/results/** | DERIVED verdicts — every script entry | the orphan qa-reports branch, main/<sha>/ and pr/<n>/<sha>/, written by the CI job qa-publish | take the base’s side: bun run cat merge:main does, then bun run cat regen | . | <instance>/test/attestations/** | JUDGEMENTS — every agent, human and baseline-pair attestation, qa-attestations/v1 | main, as authored content | a person reads both sides; never regenerated, never “take ours” | . test/results/ files are not committed on main, so a base merge conflicts there only for a branch that still carries a copy. merge:main takes the base’s side (the derived-results pattern in merge-conflict-patterns), which is the deletion, and regen rewrites the working copy. Do not hand-resolve one and do not regenerate one in order to “commit the result”: the record of a commit is its qa-reports entry, which no merge touches. Regenerating is a resolution, not a guess, because both writers are idempotent (sameScriptVerdict keeps a reproduced entry verbatim and ignores reviewed_at, reviewed_sha and script_commit_sha), so a sidecar is a pure function of the tree. A conflict in test/attestations/ is two judgements that disagree, and reconciling them is a person’s call. No merge-conflict pattern names that tree, so merge:main refuses it, as does qa:attestations:migrate. Keep both sides’ entries unless they are the same judgement; then run bun run cat qa:attestations:migrate:check, which exits 1 if a judgement is still only in a derived file. There is no qa:resolve-conflicts command: derived sidecars are not committed, so there is nothing for it to resolve.

3744.title: A change that moves a cached step’s key — publish what CI can verify
3744.content: If the change moves the key of an exact cached step whose producer the determinism audit lists as DETERMINISTIC, run bun run cat cache:publish <step> before pushing, so CI only verifies the entry instead of rebuilding it. Today that is cat-mount when index.lock.json changes. Verdicts are never published this way. The rule, the trust classes and the budget are in cache-first-ci.

3745.title: Content PRs: label content, and document the review before ready (STRICT)
3745.content: Owner, 2026-11-15: “content PRs get a label and that indicates a content review process needs to be documented as part of making it ready”. What is content. A PR is a content PR when it changes folio content text or what a reader of the folio sees as its substance: block wording, tables, figures and the models they are drawn from (ArchiMate, BPMN, DMN), glossary terms and definitions, references, a change set (CS-), a public comment response, or a re-derivation of a content layer’s generated summaries. It is not content when it changes only harness or tool code, workflows, pins (index.lock.json), work items, tests or docs about the platform. A PR that regenerates a content table or figure from its source is content too: what the reader sees changes. When in doubt, label it content; the owner can take the label off. What the agent does. | Label it content when you open it (or as soon as you see it is content). The label exists in every content repository; create it with colour 0e8a16 if a new repository lacks it. | Open it as a draft, and keep it a draft until the review is documented. Never merge it, and never ask the merge manager to: content is the owner’s or the committee’s decision (merge-manager-watcher §”Safety rules”). | Before marking it ready, add a ## Content review section to the PR body that says which review process it went through and points to its record. One or more of: . | the owner’s decision card id (Q-…) approving the wording, or a corpus-gate waiver card; | the committee decision or public-comment review-log entry (a link); | the editing-hci-validation instance of the changed blocks (its path or work item), the record check:corpus-gate reads; | the review page of the preview with its verdicts (a link), and the review coverage numbers of §”Recipe” step 5. Say what is still open, if anything. A placeholder (“TODO”, “pending”) is not a record. Never invent a review step that did not happen: a recorded waiver is better than a made-up history. | . | Then mark it ready. merge:guard check 9 (content-review) reads that section: a content draft without it is pending, and a content PR marked ready without it is a failure. | . Keep functional changes out of it. A code, configuration, pin, schema, CI or tooling change found inside a content PR is split into its own non-content PR, and removed from the content PR with an ordinary revert commit. Bring a content PR up to current main only after every repository it depends on is stable (merge-manager-watcher §”Merging across dependent repositories”, rules 4 and 5). What the merge manager does. merge:watch, both the report and --queue, leaves out every PR labelled content, so content never appears in the merge manager’s status table, even with ready-to-merge on it. Content PRs go to the owner one by one, by card.

3746.title: Shipping is not merging — hand over on the PR itself
3746.content: A PR is handed over when it is ready to merge as defined in merge-queue §”What ‘ready to merge’ means”. What happens after the handover is merge-to-main, called by merge-train.bpmn for a queued PR and by crdm-close.bpmn for a CRDM feature. When the branch is green and pushed, it reaches the Merge Steward only by its own state: label ready-to-merge, a signed ready: <head sha> comment, and no needs-merge-human. merge-queue §”Handing a PR to the queue” has the six points, and when NOT to spend CI keeping up while far back. The PR’s state is the record. The request to merge is a message: send the merge manager the six-line merge request of merge-manager-watcher §”The merge request: six lines”, with the PR URL, the session URL, what changed, the rendered preview and what to look for in it (owner ruling, 2026-11-07). Never merge it yourself, and never re-pin to make it green: send repin+merge: instead (owner ruling, 2026-11-13). A lone session is elected merge manager alone, so it posts the same six lines in its own chat, then asks the owner by card.

3747.title: Opening the PR (only when asked)
3747.content: GitHub access here is via the GitHub MCP server, whose tools are deferred (lazy-loaded). At session start they appear as names only — you cannot call them until you load the schema: . ToolSearch "select:mcp__github__create_pull_request" . Then call mcp__github__create_pull_request with owner, repo, head (the feature branch), base. This “load-then-call” round-trip is by design, not a failure, and is needed once per deferred tool per session, for every mcp__github__* tool (review, comment, merge, CI status). PR body content: pr-description, written for a first-time reader. PR body convention: end with the Claude Code footer + session link (see the harness git instructions). Do not include the model identifier in the PR.

3748.title: Guardrails
3748.content: . | Never push to the default branch and never merge a PR without an explicit ask. Prepare-merge leaves the decision to the human. When the ask comes, the merge runs merge-to-main; a broad instruction such as “fix all issues until green” is not the ask. | In folio-assistant an agent never merges to main at all. When CI is green on every job: mark the PR Ready for review, add the label ready-to-merge, and comment ready: <head sha>. The Merge Steward session brings main in, regenerates and merges. If it reports red: fix, then re-label. The policy is in continual-progress §”Green means handed to the Merge Steward”. | Check the change against the skills that govern it before calling it ready, an agent’s PR above all. Green CI says the code does what its tests say; it does not say the change keeps the rules the owner set for that area. Read the governing skills (from the mounted layers when the MCP skill server is unreachable) and hold the diff to them: a step that, say, copies the IG Publisher’s finished HTML into a site passes every test and breaks ig-render-jekyll. A design choice the PR body describes in passing is a question for the owner when a skill already answers it, never an implementation detail to merge past. | --force-with-lease, never bare --force when a rebase rewrote history. | Honest green. Pre-existing red is reported as pre-existing, with evidence; your-change red blocks the “ready” claim. | NO CHECKS IS NOT GREEN — verify against the run list, never the PR page. A PR with zero check runs renders identically to one whose checks have not started. Both are “nothing red”. A push followed by a PR can produce no pull_request-event run for that head, the newest run on the branch being for the previous head. Waiting longer is not the remedy, because how long you wait does not predict whether a run appears, and neither is avoiding force-pushes: plain fast-forwards hit it too. So before calling a branch ready, and before any merge: . | Read mergeable_state FIRST — and believe it only when it says dirty. clean can be served stale (a merged PR’s pre-merge view), and unknown means GitHub has not finished computing it. dirty is the one value worth acting on unilaterally, because its remedy — merging the base in — costs nothing on a PR that did not need it. dirty means the PR conflicts with its base, which is very likely why nothing ran: a workflow on: pull_request: with actions/checkout@v4 and no ref: checks out refs/pull/N/merge, and a conflicting PR has no such commit. When it is dirty, merge the base branch in — do NOT dispatch. A workflow_dispatch run resolves refs/heads/<branch>, so it tests the branch, not the merge result: on a conflicted PR that is a green signal for a tree that will never exist. The workaround in step 3 is for a MERGEABLE PR whose run never fired. | Read the PR’s head_sha. | mcp__github__actions_list → list_workflow_runs, filtered by branch, and find a run whose head_sha matches. | No run for that sha → the branch is NOT ready, whatever the PR page shows. Say so in those words rather than “checks pending”, and re-run them with mcp__github__actions_run_trigger → run_workflow against the branch. | Re-check after every push. A new commit moves the head, and the head is what the absence attaches to. | . An agent holding a standing merge authorisation must not read zero checks as nothing-red: could-not-determine is never rendered as clean, at the merge decision as everywhere else. | One branch. Develop on the assigned claude/* branch; moving work to a different branch needs explicit permission. | NEVER DELETE A FEATURE OR branches/ BRANCH without explicit assent from the user or the repository owner. Not after a merge, not as cleanup, not to quiet a tool that complains about it, and never by passing --delete-branch or its API equivalent. A merged branch is still the record of how the work was done, the base a revert or a follow-up is cut from, and the ref a staging deploy is served under. Deleting it is irreversible from the agent’s side and buys nothing the owner asked for. The same rule is in prepare-merge-auto.md Phase 4 and the anti-patterns, because an agent following either skill must meet it. If you change one copy, change the other. When a tool or hook complains about a branch, fix the tool — for example a reachability check in a stop hook — never delete the branch. | .

3750.title: Publish verification, and the one alert
3750.content: Skill publish-verification: Verify what a publish produced, and alert the publication manager whenever any step after the publish button fails — the verifier set, how to add a verifier, what is in scope, and how the publication manager triages the one alert. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release, Adjudicate two KG extractors, GuidelineKG nightly path: verify and adjudicate the result, GuidelineKG nightly path: prepare the work order, GuidelineKG nightly path . The verifier set runs over the built site before it is deployed. It does not stop the deploy: its outcome is judged after the push, and any failure reaches the publication manager through the same single alert as every other step after the publish button.

3751.title: The two processes
3751.content: . | publish-verification.bpmn — the verifier set over the built tree, between the export and the deploy. Pass, fail, or could-not-tell; the caller deploys either way and judges the outcome after the push. | publish-alert.bpmn — ONE alert, called from every failure edge in docs-site-publish.bpmn: a refused security gate, a failed deploy, a lost preview, a failed built-site check. It reaches the role that already owns the release: the publication manager. | .

3752.title: The verifier set
3752.content: bun run cat publish:verify -- --dir <built site> [--report out.md] — scripts/publish-verify.ts. Exit 0 pass · 1 a finding · 2 could not tell. The caller treats 1 and 2 alike: an unverified release is not a verified one. Each verifier is one entry in VERIFIERS: an id, the question it asks, and a function from the directory to findings. Adding a verifier is adding an entry; the report, the exit code and the alert need no change. Give it a test that builds a document to break it, as publish-verify.test.ts does. jsonld-expand is the first: every JSON-LD document of ours is expanded by a real processor (jsonld.js, network refused). A key the @context does not declare is DROPPED by a processor, silently.

3753.title: A verifier the preview cannot ask is a release failure waiting (STRICT)
3753.content: The staging preview runs the same verifier set, so a preview is never greener than the release it previews. That promise breaks wherever the preview answers a different question. It serves the PUBLISHED search index (--search-index borrowed), so search-index there asks only “present and parsing”, never “does it cover the pages” — so a preview can be green while the release refuses it. So the preview asks the coverage question of the index it built, before swapping in the published one: publish-verify.ts --dir ./_site --only search-index. The rule, for any verifier added later: if the preview substitutes an input, the verifier runs on the preview’s own input before the substitution. A check only the release asks fails after merge, on main, where everyone pays for it. Deliberate exclusion is marked in what is built. search_exclude: true is front matter, and front matter is gone after Jekyll. head_custom.html writes <meta name="fa-search-exclude"> for it, and search-index leaves those pages out of the coverage denominator and COUNTS them in its finding. An exclusion the built page does not carry cannot be told from a truncated index, and the release check will refuse it, correctly.

3754.title: What is in scope
3754.content: A document is ours when its @context names our content context or binds a namespace in the own-namespaces code list. Everything else in the tree — an ingested IG’s artefact index, for example — is counted as out of scope, reported, and never able to block the release.

3755.title: Triage, for the publication manager
3755.content: The alert is a tracking issue labelled publication-manager: opened on the first failure, commented on for each later one (a comment notifies; an edit does not), closed by the next clean publish. The issue says which step failed and whether the site deployed: . | Nothing was deployed (the export, or verification) — the live site is the previous publish. Hold, or fix forward. | The site deployed and something after it failed (a lost preview) — it is live. Say so in the issue before fixing. | . The label names the role, not a person: no actor declares a GitHub account for publication-manager. Watching the label is how a person takes the role.

3757.title: QA report signing — two routes, chosen by the performer’s reach
3757.content: Named by: Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . A QA report becomes evidence when a third party can establish what was measured and who vouches for it. folio-test-run/v1 (schemas/sdlc/test-run.ts) answers the first: a data hash and a process hash, each all-or-nothing, plus the skill it tests, whose contract its recorded cases are checked against (test-run-conforms). This skill answers the second, and it has two routes because the participant doing the signing may not be able to reach anything: some machine actors are air-gapped, an API cannot be called from one, and a human actor signs instead. The subject signed is the QA report. This skill builds on signing. That skill holds what is true of any signature: who signs, what is signed, which suites a trust anchor accepts, key custody, the route, and what a verifier must check and record. This one keeps only what is particular to QA reports: the run hashes, the qa-reports branch, and the line between attestation and certification. Where the two overlap, signing is the rule.

3758.title: The process is executable — do not hand-roll the branch
3758.content: sdlc/processes/qa-report-signing.bpmn, with the branch computed by decisions/signing-route.dmn. Run it with workflow_start / workflow_next / workflow_complete like every other diagram here. The gateway refuses a hand-supplied outcome: the route is a consequence of declared facts, not a preference.

3759.title: Reach is a property of the ACTOR, and unknown is a third state
3759.content: schemas/process/actor-reach.ts. | One vocabulary, two levels. An actor’s reach uses the same scale as the deployment’s network — internet, egress-restricted, air-gapped. There is no second scale, because two spellings of one fact drift apart. | Composition is asymmetric. An air-gapped deployment forces every actor air-gapped. A connected one forces nothing — a connected site may hold an isolated signing host. So an actor that declares no reach inside a connected deployment is unknown, not internet. | unknown routes to the human. A gateway that read could-not-determine as “use the API” would fail closed on the wire and open in the record: the call fails and what survives is an unsigned report that nothing marks as unsigned. Could-not-check is never green. | .

3760.title: Reach is declared, not a capability
3760.content: There is no network-egress capability. A capability is an environment probe — detection: { method: "command", … }, a thing you run to find out. Reach is an architectural fact, declared by whoever built the site. On an air-gapped host a failed probe is indistinguishable from an outage, and the safe reading of an outage (“retry later”) is the unsafe reading of an air gap. A capability would also carry the same fact as reach in a second place, free to disagree. What is a probe is whether an endpoint is configured: signing-api, an env-var detection. The DMN table reads both, because they answer different questions — can this host call out and is there anything to call. A configured endpoint on an air-gapped host is still uncallable.

3761.title: Declaration and execution are different mechanisms
3761.content: qa-report-signing.ts declares: . requiredCapabilities: [ { capabilityId: "signing-api", degradation: "fallback", fallbackRole: "publication-manager" }, ], . fallbackRole says which lane takes over when no capability can do it. It does not route anything, and nothing executes it; the gateway is what executes. They must agree — the declaration is what a reader and check:fallback-roles can see without executing anything; the gateway is what happens. Where they disagree, the diagram is what ran, and the declaration is the bug.

3762.title: Recording the attestation
3762.content: Record what signing §6 requires (suite, key, anchor, result, when checked) and, above all, which route signed it, not only that it is signed. The two are not interchangeable: one attests that a service with a key saw these hashes, the other that a person holding release authority did.

3763.title: Where the signed report goes: the qa-reports branch, next to its run
3763.content: A QA report is a derived record — it can be rebuilt from the tree and the data it hashed — so it is kept where every derived QA result is kept: the orphan qa-reports branch, in the entry keyed by the commit it judged (main/<sha>/ or pr/<n>/<sha>/), written through scripts/qa-store.ts and never by a hand git push. The signature and the route that produced it travel with the report, in the same entry, because a signature separated from the bytes it covers attests nothing a reader can check. Task_RecordAttestation in qa-report-signing.bpmn ends there. What does not go there. A certification — an accountable role’s Decision taken on a test report’s rollup — is a separate node, and it stays on main beside the attestations: it is a judgement, the same class as test/attestations/, and no regeneration can reproduce it. That decision belongs to the test-plan process, which calls this one to sign; this skill only signs. A read of a signed report follows the store’s rules: a miss is never read as “unsigned and fine”, and a store that cannot answer is UNKNOWN, which routes like unknown reach — to a person, never to a pass.
